en.title: The Suez Canal officially opens
en.text:
On 17 November 1869, a line of ships led by the French imperial yacht L'Aigle, carrying Empress Eugénie, sailed into the new Suez Canal. For the first time, ships could travel from the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea without going all the way around Africa.

The idea was ancient. Pharaohs and later Persian and Arab rulers had dug canals linking the Nile to the Red Sea, but none joined the two seas directly. In 1854 the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps won a concession from Egypt's ruler Sa'id Pasha, and digging began in April 1859.

The work took ten years. In the early years it relied on forced labour: tens of thousands of Egyptian peasants were made to dig by hand in desert heat, and many died from disease and exhaustion. Later, steam dredgers and excavators did much of the work. The finished canal was about 164 kilometres long, with no locks, because the two seas sit at almost the same level.

The opening was a grand international celebration, with kings, scientists and journalists invited by Khedive Isma'il. Yet the cost pushed Egypt deep into debt. In 1875 Egypt sold its shares to Britain, and in 1882 Britain occupied the country, partly to control the canal.

The canal changed the map of the world. The sea route from London to Mumbai became thousands of kilometres shorter, and ports on the East African coast, from Mombasa to Zanzibar, were suddenly much closer to Europe. That speed also made it easier for European powers to reach, trade with and later colonise Africa and Asia.

In 1956 Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the canal, leading to the Suez Crisis, when Britain, France and Israel invaded and were forced to withdraw under international pressure. The canal was closed again from 1967 to 1975 after war with Israel. Today it has been widened and deepened, and roughly one in ten of the world's traded goods passes through it. When the giant container ship Ever Given got stuck there for six days in 2021, world trade felt the shock.

fr.title: Ouverture officielle du canal de Suez
fr.text: Le canal de Suez est officiellement inauguré en Égypte, reliant la mer Méditerranée à la mer Rouge. Les navires allant d'Europe vers l'Asie et l'Afrique de l'Est n'ont plus besoin de contourner le cap de Bonne-Espérance. Sa construction a duré environ dix ans (1859–1869) et il reste aujourd'hui l'une des routes maritimes les plus importantes du monde.

ar.title: الافتتاح الرسمي لقناة السويس
ar.text: افتُتحت قناة السويس رسميًا في مصر، لتربط البحر الأبيض المتوسط بالبحر الأحمر. ولم تعد السفن المتجهة من أوروبا إلى آسيا وشرق أفريقيا بحاجة إلى الدوران حول رأس الرجاء الصالح. استغرق بناؤها نحو عشر سنوات (1859–1869)، ولا تزال حتى اليوم من أهم طرق الملاحة في العالم.

ko.title: 수에즈 운하 공식 개통
ko.text: 이집트에서 수에즈 운하가 공식 개통되어 지중해와 홍해가 연결되었습니다. 유럽에서 아시아와 동아프리카로 가는 배들은 더 이상 희망봉을 돌아갈 필요가 없게 되었습니다. 건설에는 약 10년(1859–1869)이 걸렸으며, 오늘날에도 세계에서 가장 중요한 해상 항로 중 하나입니다.

ja.title: スエズ運河が正式に開通
ja.text: エジプトでスエズ運河が正式に開通し、地中海と紅海が結ばれました。ヨーロッパからアジアや東アフリカへ向かう船は、もう喜望峰を回る必要がなくなりました。建設には約10年(1859〜1869年)かかり、今も世界で最も重要な航路の一つです。

zh.title: 苏伊士运河正式通航
zh.text: 苏伊士运河在埃及正式通航,连接了地中海和红海。从欧洲前往亚洲和东非的船只不再需要绕行好望角。运河修建历时约十年(1859–1869年),至今仍是世界上最重要的航运通道之一。

es.title: Se inaugura oficialmente el canal de Suez
es.text: El canal de Suez se inauguró oficialmente en Egipto, uniendo el mar Mediterráneo con el mar Rojo. Los barcos que viajaban de Europa a Asia y África Oriental ya no tenían que rodear el cabo de Buena Esperanza. Su construcción duró unos diez años (1859–1869) y hoy sigue siendo una de las rutas marítimas más importantes del mundo.

sw.title: Mfereji wa Suez wafunguliwa rasmi
sw.text: Mfereji wa Suez ulifunguliwa rasmi nchini Misri, ukiunganisha Bahari ya Mediterania na Bahari ya Shamu. en.title: Lunokhod 1: the first robot to roam the Moon
en.text:
On 17 November 1970, the Soviet spacecraft Luna 17 landed in the Sea of Rains (Mare Imbrium) on the Moon. A ramp folded down, and an eight-wheeled machine rolled onto the grey dust. Lunokhod 1, whose name means "Moon walker", became the first remote-controlled robot to explore another world.

Lunokhod looked like a bathtub on wheels with a lid. The lid opened in the lunar day to expose solar panels that charged its batteries. During the two-week lunar night, when temperatures fall far below minus 150 °C, the lid closed and a small radioactive heater kept its electronics alive.

There was no autopilot. A team of five drivers sat in a control room in Crimea, nearly 400,000 kilometres away. Every command took several seconds to travel there and back, so they drove slowly, studying a new television picture before each move, always afraid of craters and boulders.

The robot was meant to work for three months. It lasted about ten, until September 1971. It travelled roughly 10.5 kilometres, sent back more than 20,000 pictures and over 200 panoramas, tested the lunar soil at hundreds of places, and studied cosmic rays and X-rays from space.

Lunokhod 1 also carried a laser reflector. For decades scientists could not find it, until in 2010 American researchers located the rover in new orbital photographs and bounced a laser off it again. The little reflector still helps measure the exact distance between Earth and the Moon.

The rover proved that machines could explore other worlds for months, guided from Earth. Every rover that has since rolled across the Moon or Mars, from China's Yutu to NASA's Perseverance, follows the path it opened.

es.text: El Lunokhod 1 de la Unión Soviética llegó a la Luna a bordo de la Luna 17 y se convirtió en el primer robot en recorrer la superficie de otro mundo, guiado por operadores desde la Tierra.

en.title: The origin of International Students' Day
en.text:
International Students' Day is marked around the world on 17 November. It began with tragedy in Prague in 1939, when students paid with their lives for resisting occupation.

In March 1939 Nazi Germany occupied what remained of Czechoslovakia. On 28 October, the anniversary of Czechoslovak independence, crowds in Prague protested. Police and soldiers fired on them. A young medical student, Jan Opletal, was shot in the stomach and died on 11 November.

His funeral on 15 November became another protest, with thousands of students singing the national anthem. The Nazi leadership used it as an excuse to crush the universities. Before dawn on 17 November 1939, troops raided student residences. Nine student leaders and teachers were executed without trial. Around 1,200 students were sent to the Sachsenhausen concentration camp, and all Czech universities and colleges were closed for the rest of the war.

In 1941, students who had escaped to London, together with the International Students' Council, declared 17 November International Students' Day, to honour the victims and to stand for the right to education and freedom.

The date returned to history fifty years later. On 17 November 1989 students in Prague marched to remember 1939. Riot police beat them, and the anger that followed grew into the peaceful Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia within weeks.

Today the day is used by student unions worldwide to talk about access to education, free speech and student welfare. It is a reminder that young people in classrooms have often been the first to stand up when freedom is threatened.

en.title: Uhuru: the night Tanganyika became free
en.place: Dar es Salaam and Kilimanjaro, Tanganyika
en.text:
## Midnight in the stadium

On the night of 8 December 1961, a huge crowd filled the new national stadium in Dar es Salaam. Just before midnight, the lights were switched off. In the darkness, the British Union Jack was lowered. When the lights came back on, a new flag was flying: green for the land, black for the people, and gold for the country's mineral wealth. The crowd roared. It was 9 December, and Tanganyika was independent.

Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, represented Queen Elizabeth II. Prime Minister Julius Nyerere, aged 39, led the new nation.

## The long road

Tanganyika's borders were drawn by colonial powers. Germany conquered the territory from the 1880s against fierce resistance, including the Hehe wars and the Maji Maji uprising. After the First World War, Britain took over, governing under international trusteeship.

The independence struggle was led by TANU, founded in 1954. Through mass organisation, peaceful pressure and clever use of the UN system, TANU won overwhelming election victories in 1958–59 and 1960. Self-government followed in May 1961, then independence.

## A candle on Kilimanjaro

Years earlier, Nyerere had said that the people wished to light a candle and put it on top of Mount Kilimanjaro, to shine beyond the borders, giving hope where there was despair, love where there was hate, and dignity where before there had only been humiliation.

On independence night that promise was kept. A team led by army officer Lieutenant Alexander Nyirenda climbed Kilimanjaro, planted the new flag on the summit, and lit a torch. The highest point of the mountain, until then named after the German emperor, became Uhuru Peak.

The Uhuru Torch, Mwenge wa Uhuru, has been carried across Tanzania every year since, visiting every region, opening development projects and carrying messages of unity, peace and hard work.

## The new nation

Tanganyika at independence was one of the poorest countries in the world. Life expectancy was around 40 years. Most people were farmers. There were very few secondary schools, and only a handful of Tanganyikans had university degrees. At independence the country had only around a dozen African doctors.

Nyerere named three enemies: poverty, ignorance and disease. The new government set out to expand schools, clinics, roads and water supplies.

In January 1962 Nyerere surprised everyone by resigning as prime minister to rebuild TANU and connect the party to ordinary people. Rashidi Kawawa became prime minister. On 9 December 1962, exactly one year after independence, Tanganyika became a republic, and Nyerere was elected its first president.

## Early challenges

Independence was not easy. In January 1964 soldiers of the Tanganyika Rifles mutinied over pay and the continued presence of British officers. Nyerere, to his great embarrassment, had to ask British marines to restore order. He then rebuilt the army as the Tanzania People's Defence Force, closely tied to the nation.

In April 1964 Tanganyika united with Zanzibar, and the new country took the name Tanzania later that year.

In 1967, the Arusha Declaration set out a path of socialism and self-reliance, Ujamaa, nationalising banks and major industries. That path brought achievements in education, health and national unity, and also serious economic difficulties.

## A peaceful nation

One of independence's greatest achievements was peace. Tanzania, with more than 120 ethnic groups, has avoided the ethnic conflicts that tore apart many countries. Historians credit the shared language, Kiswahili, the policies of Nyerere's government that discouraged tribalism, and the inclusive national identity built from TANU's struggle.

## Different views

Some critics argue that the one-party state created after independence limited political freedom and that economic policies held the country back. Others emphasise the dignity, unity and stability that independence brought. Most Tanzanians today celebrate 9 December as the beginning of their nation's story, while debating how best to fulfil its promise.

## Celebrating Uhuru

Independence Day, 9 December, is Tanzania's national day. Celebrations include parades, speeches and, often, the arrival of the Uhuru Torch. Uhuru Peak remains the goal of tens of thousands of climbers each year, each one standing where the candle of freedom was first lit.

## The independence constitution

Tanganyika became independent under a constitution modelled on the British parliamentary system. Queen Elizabeth II remained head of state, represented by a governor-general, Sir Richard Turnbull, who had been the last colonial governor. Real power lay with the prime minister and the elected National Assembly. This arrangement lasted only one year before Tanganyika became a republic with an executive president.

## Joining the world

On 14 December 1961, just five days after independence, Tanganyika was admitted as a member of the United Nations. For a country that had been a UN trust territory, it was a moment of special pride: the people who had once petitioned the UN now sat in its General Assembly as equals. Tanganyika also joined the Commonwealth and quickly became an active voice for African liberation.

## Building the institutions

The new government faced a huge shortage of trained people. Many senior posts in the civil service, police and army were held by Europeans. The government launched Africanisation, training and promoting Tanganyikans as quickly as possible.

Education was a top priority. The University College, Dar es Salaam, opened in October 1961, beginning with a faculty of law in a building borrowed from TANU. It later became the University of Dar es Salaam, one of Africa's leading universities and a centre of debate on African development in the 1960s and 1970s.

## Celebrations across the land

Independence was celebrated not only in Dar es Salaam. In towns and villages across Tanganyika, people gathered around radios, held dances and feasts, and raised the new flag. Schools held ceremonies, and churches and mosques offered prayers. For many older people, who remembered German rule, Maji Maji and the hardships of the colonial era, the moment was deeply emotional.

## Kiswahili and the national culture

After independence, Kiswahili was promoted as the national language, used in government, schools and the media. National culture was encouraged through music, dance, poetry and theatre. A Ministry of National Culture and Youth was created in 1962. These policies helped build a shared Tanzanian identity across the country's many peoples.

## Dar es Salaam: the haven of peace

The city where independence was declared has its own history. In the 1860s, Sultan Majid of Zanzibar began building a new town on a sheltered harbour on the mainland and named it Dar es Salaam, from Arabic meaning "house" or "haven of peace". After his death the town declined, until the Germans made it the capital of their colony in 1891. Under British rule it remained the capital.

At independence Dar es Salaam was a city of around 130,000 people. Today it is one of Africa's largest cities, with several million inhabitants. In 1973 the government decided to move the capital to Dodoma, in the centre of the country, and the move of government offices was largely completed in the late 2010s, though Dar es Salaam remains the country's commercial heart.

## What independence meant for ordinary people

For farmers in the villages, independence did not change daily life overnight. But it brought new schools, clinics and wells in the following years, and the right to vote for their own leaders. For many it meant dignity: no longer being treated as second-class people in their own land, with jobs and opportunities once reserved for Europeans now open to them.

Many older Tanzanians remember the songs, the flags in every village, and the feeling that the future now belonged to them.

## Key people

Julius Nyerere: leader of TANU, first prime minister and president.
Rashidi Kawawa: TANU leader and trade unionist, prime minister from January 1962 and later vice-president.
Bibi Titi Mohammed: organiser of TANU's women, whose mobilisation made the movement a mass force.
Oscar Kambona: TANU's secretary-general during the struggle and a minister after independence.
Sir Richard Turnbull: the last colonial governor, who cooperated with TANU and became governor-general.
Alexander Nyirenda: the army officer who planted the flag and lit the torch on Kilimanjaro.

## Timeline

1885: Germany begins claiming the territory through the German East Africa Company.
1891: The German government takes direct control of German East Africa.
1905–1907: The Maji Maji uprising is crushed.
1919–1922: After the First World War, Britain takes over Tanganyika under a League of Nations mandate.
1946: Tanganyika becomes a United Nations trust territory.
1954: TANU is founded on 7 July with Julius Nyerere as president.
1955: Nyerere addresses the UN Trusteeship Council in New York.
1958–1959: TANU and its allies sweep the first elections.
1960: TANU wins 70 of 71 seats; Nyerere becomes chief minister.
May 1961: Internal self-government; Nyerere becomes prime minister.
9 December 1961: Independence; the flag is raised and the Uhuru Torch is lit on Kilimanjaro.
14 December 1961: Tanganyika joins the United Nations.
9 December 1962: Tanganyika becomes a republic with Nyerere as president.
26 April 1964: Union with Zanzibar; later that year the country is named Tanzania.

## Sources

John Iliffe, A Modern History of Tanganyika (1979). Julius Nyerere, Freedom and Unity (1967). Issa Shivji and others, Development as Rebellion: A Biography of Julius Nyerere (2020).

en.title: The Union: how Tanganyika and Zanzibar became Tanzania
en.text:
## A handful of soil

In April 1964, President Julius Nyerere of Tanganyika and President Abeid Amani Karume of Zanzibar mixed soil from the mainland and the islands together in a single vessel. The gesture symbolised the birth of a new nation. On 26 April 1964, the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar came into being. Six months later it took the name Tanzania.

## Two lands, one family

The mainland and the islands are separated by a channel only about 40 kilometres wide. For a thousand years, boats crossed it carrying traders, fishermen, families and ideas. The Swahili coast and the islands shared Kiswahili, Islam, music, food and family ties.

Under the Omani sultans, Zanzibar ruled parts of the mainland coast. The caravan routes from the interior ended at Bagamoyo and Kilwa, facing the islands. In the colonial era, Germany and Britain separated them politically, but many people moved back and forth.

## Why unite in 1964

Several forces pushed toward union.

Pan-Africanism: Nyerere believed deeply in African unity, and once even offered to delay Tanganyika's independence if it would help form an East African federation with Kenya and Uganda. That larger federation did not happen. The union with Zanzibar was a smaller step toward the ideal.

Security: Zanzibar's revolution in January 1964 had been chaotic. Karume's government was fragile and divided between moderate and radical factions. Union with the larger, stable mainland offered protection.

The Cold War: Zanzibar's revolutionary government quickly built ties with East Germany, the Soviet Union and China. Western governments feared a communist base in East Africa. Nyerere also worried about foreign powers using the islands. Union brought Zanzibar into a non-aligned, stable state.

## The Articles of Union

On 22 April 1964 Nyerere and Karume signed the Articles of Union in Zanzibar. The agreement was negotiated quickly and in secret among a few leaders, which has led to debates ever since about how it was made.

The union created an unusual structure: two governments rather than one or three. There is a Union government, responsible for "Union matters", and a separate Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar, with its own president and later its own House of Representatives, responsible for everything else in Zanzibar. Mainland affairs that are not union matters are handled by the Union government itself.

At first there were eleven union matters, including the constitution, foreign affairs, defence, police, citizenship and external trade. Over the years, the list grew to more than twenty.

Nyerere became president of the United Republic, and Karume the first vice-president.

## A new name

The new country needed a name. A public competition was held, and the name Tanzania, combining TANganyika and ZANzibar, with the ending "ia", was adopted on 29 October 1964.

## Building one nation

In 1977 the ruling parties of both sides, TANU and the Afro-Shirazi Party, merged into Chama Cha Mapinduzi, CCM, strengthening the political union. A national flag combines the green of Tanganyika's flag with the blue of the sea, divided by a black diagonal band edged in gold.

## Tensions and debates

The union has survived for more than sixty years, one of the very few lasting unions of independent African states. But it has faced repeated tensions.

Some Zanzibaris feel the union gives too much power to the mainland and that Zanzibar's autonomy has shrunk as more matters became union affairs. Debates continue over revenue sharing, oil and gas, and Zanzibar's right to join international organisations. Some mainlanders, meanwhile, argue that the mainland has no government of its own.

In 1984 Zanzibar's president Aboud Jumbe was forced to resign after pushing for a looser union. In 2013 a constitutional review commission led by former prime minister Joseph Warioba proposed a three-government structure, with separate governments for Tanganyika, Zanzibar and the Union. The proposal was debated intensely, but the two-government structure was kept in the draft constitution.

## Different views

Supporters see the union as a model of African unity and a source of peace, security and shared identity. Critics argue that it was created without consulting the people and needs reform. Most Tanzanians, whatever their views on its structure, regard the union as part of who they are.

## Union Day

26 April is celebrated as Union Day, Siku ya Muungano, with national ceremonies. The image of the two presidents mixing soil remains one of the most famous symbols of Tanzanian nationhood.

## Making the union legal

The Articles of Union were ratified by the Parliament of Tanganyika on 25 April 1964 and by Zanzibar's Revolutionary Council. An interim constitution followed in 1965, and the permanent Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania was adopted in 1977, the same year TANU and the ASP merged into CCM.

## How it works in daily life

Under the union, citizens of Tanzania share one citizenship, one passport, one army, one currency and one foreign policy. Zanzibar has its own president, government, House of Representatives, courts for many matters, and its own flag and anthem alongside the national ones.

The president of Zanzibar is a member of the Union cabinet. Zanzibar elects members to the Union parliament in Dodoma. Ferries and flights link Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar many times a day, and many families live and work on both sides.

## Why other unions failed

Africa has seen many attempts at political union. Egypt and Syria formed the United Arab Republic in 1958, but Syria left in 1961. Senegal and the Gambia formed the Senegambia Confederation in 1982; it was dissolved in 1989. The first East African Community of Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, sharing services such as railways, airways and posts, collapsed in 1977 amid political disputes. A new East African Community was founded in 2000 and has since grown to include several more countries.

Against this background, the Tanzanian union's survival for more than six decades is remarkable. Historians point to shared language and culture, the dominance of one ruling party on both sides, and the flexibility of the two-government structure as reasons.

## The union and the region

The union made Tanzania a larger, more secure state, able to play a major role in East and southern Africa. It also removed a possible flashpoint of the Cold War from the region. For pan-Africanists, it remains proof that African states can choose to unite.

## Looking ahead

Debates about the union are part of normal political life in Tanzania. Questions about the sharing of oil and gas revenues, the powers of Zanzibar, and the structure of government will continue. But for most Tanzanians, the union is no longer simply an agreement of 1964; it is the country they were born into.

## Nyerere and Karume

The union depended greatly on the relationship between its two founders. Julius Nyerere, a university-educated teacher and thinker, and Abeid Amani Karume, a former sailor and boat-owner who had risen through workers' and community politics in Zanzibar, came from very different backgrounds. They did not always agree, and Karume guarded Zanzibar's autonomy jealously. But both were committed to keeping the union together, and their partnership carried it through its first difficult years.

## Symbols of one nation

The national flag, adopted in 1964, combines the green of Tanganyika's flag and the blue of Zanzibar's, divided by a black band with gold edges. The coat of arms shows a man and a woman, a warrior's shield, the torch of freedom, crossed spear and tools, and Mount Kilimanjaro at its base, with the motto Uhuru na Umoja, Freedom and Unity.

The national anthem, "Mungu Ibariki Afrika", God Bless Africa, set to the melody also used in South Africa and elsewhere, is sung in Kiswahili on both the mainland and the islands.

## Key people

Julius Nyerere: president of Tanganyika, then first president of the United Republic.
Abeid Amani Karume: president of Zanzibar and first vice-president of the union.
Rashidi Kawawa: second vice-president of the union and a close ally of Nyerere.
Aboud Jumbe: Karume's successor as president of Zanzibar, who later pushed for a looser union.
Joseph Warioba: former prime minister who led the 2013 constitutional review commission.

## Timeline

10 December 1963: Zanzibar becomes independent under the Sultan.
12 January 1964: The Zanzibar Revolution; Abeid Karume becomes president.
22 April 1964: Nyerere and Karume sign the Articles of Union.
25 April 1964: The Parliament of Tanganyika ratifies the union.
26 April 1964: The United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar is born.
29 October 1964: The name United Republic of Tanzania is adopted.
1965: An interim constitution is adopted.
7 April 1972: President Karume is assassinated in Zanzibar.
5 February 1977: TANU and the Afro-Shirazi Party merge to form CCM; a permanent constitution is adopted.
1984: Zanzibar president Aboud Jumbe resigns amid disputes over the union's structure.
1992: Multi-party politics returns to Tanzania.
2013–2014: The Warioba commission proposes three governments; the two-government structure is kept.

## Sources

Issa G. Shivji, Pan-Africanism or Pragmatism? Lessons of Tanganyika-Zanzibar Union (2008). Amrit Wilson, US Foreign Policy and Revolution: The Creation of Tanzania (1989). Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania (1977).

en.title: The Zanzibar Revolution of 1964
en.text:
## Before dawn on 12 January

In the early hours of 12 January 1964, a few hundred armed men attacked the police headquarters at Ziwani and the armoury at Mtoni on the island of Unguja. They seized weapons and moved on Zanzibar town. By the next day the government of the Sultan had collapsed. Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah fled on his yacht. Zanzibar was declared a people's republic.

## Islands of trade and division

For centuries Zanzibar was a meeting place of Africa, Arabia, Persia and India. Under the Omani sultans of the nineteenth century, it became the capital of a trading empire built on cloves and the slave trade. Arab families owned most of the large clove plantations; South Asian merchants controlled much of the trade and finance. The African majority, including descendants of enslaved people and the long-established Shirazi communities, mostly worked the land or in the towns.

Britain made Zanzibar a protectorate in 1890, ruling through the Sultan. In the 1950s, as independence approached, politics split largely along these lines of race and class.

## Elections and frustration

The Zanzibar Nationalist Party (ZNP), led by Ali Muhsin and supported by many Arabs and some Africans, called for a multi-racial Zanzibari nationalism under the Sultan. The Afro-Shirazi Party (ASP), led by Abeid Amani Karume, represented mainly African voters. The Zanzibar and Pemba People's Party (ZPPP) drew support especially from Pemba.

Elections in 1961 were bitter, and riots in June that year killed dozens of people. In the July 1963 election, the ASP won the most votes, about 54 percent. But because of how the constituencies were drawn, the ZNP and ZPPP coalition won 18 of the 31 seats and formed the government.

On 10 December 1963 Zanzibar became independent as a constitutional monarchy under the Sultan. To many ASP supporters, it seemed independence had simply handed power from the British to the old elite.

## The night of the revolution

Plans for an uprising had been made by groups within the ASP youth wing and others. The new government had also dismissed many policemen from the mainland, who now had weapons training and grievances.

The most visible figure of the first days was John Okello, a Ugandan-born labourer who had lived in Zanzibar and Pemba. He made dramatic radio broadcasts calling himself Field Marshal. Many historians believe the planning involved a wider network than Okello's own account suggests.

Abeid Karume, who was in Dar es Salaam at the start, returned and became president of the People's Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba, heading a Revolutionary Council. Abdulrahman Mohamed Babu, leader of the left-wing Umma Party, became a minister. Okello was sidelined and expelled within weeks.

## Violence

The revolution was accompanied by terrible violence. In the days that followed, armed groups attacked Arab and South Asian communities, especially in rural Unguja. Estimates of the dead range widely, from a few thousand to as many as twenty thousand. Thousands more were imprisoned or fled to Oman, Kenya and elsewhere. A film crew filmed some of the killings, which later appeared in the documentary "Africa Addio".

For some families, the revolution is remembered above all as a massacre. For many others, it is remembered as liberation. Both memories are real, and discussing them openly remains difficult.

## The revolutionary government

The new government took over large plantations and redistributed land, often in three-acre plots to landless families. It built housing, including the large Michenzani apartment blocks built with East German help, and expanded free education and health care. It also ruled without elections, detained opponents, and in the early years carried out forced marriages that caused deep pain.

Zanzibar's ties with East Germany, the Soviet Union and China alarmed the United States and Britain, who feared a "Cuba of Africa". Cold War fears were one reason why, just three months later, on 26 April 1964, Zanzibar united with Tanganyika to form Tanzania, with Karume as first vice-president.

Karume was assassinated in April 1972 at the ASP headquarters in Zanzibar town.

## Remembering

Mapinduzi Day, Revolution Day, is celebrated every 12 January in Zanzibar with parades, and the Mapinduzi Cup football tournament is held around the anniversary. Politics in Zanzibar today is still shaped by the memories of 1964, with deep divisions between parties often following old lines between Unguja and Pemba.

## Zanzibar under British protection

Britain declared Zanzibar a protectorate in 1890. The Sultan remained on the throne, but British officials held real power. In 1896, when a new sultan took the throne without British approval, British warships bombarded his palace. The Anglo-Zanzibar War lasted less than an hour and is often called the shortest war in recorded history.

Under British rule, the clove economy continued, slavery was slowly abolished, and the colonial administration favoured the Arab elite in government posts and education, deepening resentment among the African majority.

## The first days

In the first days of the revolution, John Okello's radio broadcasts were frightening and dramatic, announcing threats and orders in the name of the revolution. Order slowly returned as the Revolutionary Council took control and as police from mainland Tanganyika arrived at Karume's request to help keep the peace.

The Sultan and his family went into exile in Britain. Jamshid bin Abdullah lived there for decades, and in his old age was allowed to settle in Oman.

## Social change

The revolutionary government ended the political dominance of the old elite. Large estates were nationalised and land distributed to families. Free education and medical care were declared. Racial categories that had shaped colonial politics were officially abolished. Many Zanzibaris, especially from poor African families, gained land, housing and schooling for the first time.

At the same time, political parties other than the ASP were banned, and the government ruled through the Revolutionary Council with little tolerance for criticism. Many people suffered imprisonment and loss of property.

## Karume's death and after

Abeid Karume ruled Zanzibar until his assassination on 7 April 1972. He was succeeded by Aboud Jumbe. Over the following decades Zanzibar slowly moved toward elections, and multi-party politics returned in 1992. But elections in Zanzibar were repeatedly bitterly contested, with violence in 2001 that killed dozens of people.

## Reconciliation

In 2009 the two main rival leaders, President Amani Abeid Karume, son of the first president, and opposition leader Seif Sharif Hamad, agreed on a historic reconciliation, known as Maridhiano. A referendum in 2010 approved a Government of National Unity, sharing power between the main parties. The arrangement has faced difficulties, but it represented an important attempt to heal the divisions that began long before 1964.

## Pemba's story

Zanzibar is two main islands, Unguja and Pemba, and their experiences differ. Pemba is greener and grows most of Zanzibar's cloves. Its population, largely Shirazi, often voted differently from Unguja; the ZPPP, which joined the government before the revolution, drew much of its support from Pemba. After the revolution, many people on Pemba felt marginalised, and political divisions between the two islands remain visible in election results to this day.

## Historians' debate

Historians continue to debate the revolution. Some emphasise the deep injustice of the pre-revolutionary order, in which a minority held most land and power, and see the revolution as a popular uprising for equality. Others emphasise the violence, the role of a small armed group, and the decades of authoritarian rule that followed. Many argue that both are true: the revolution addressed real grievances, but at a terrible human cost, and its memory must include all its victims.

Open discussion of 1964 has become easier in recent years, with books, documentaries and testimonies from families on all sides helping Zanzibaris understand their shared past.

## Key people

Abeid Amani Karume: leader of the ASP and first president of revolutionary Zanzibar.
John Okello: Ugandan-born labourer and the most visible figure of the first days of the revolution.
Abdulrahman Mohamed Babu: leader of the Umma Party and a minister in the revolutionary government.
Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah: the last Sultan of Zanzibar, overthrown after one month on the throne.
Ali Muhsin: leader of the Zanzibar Nationalist Party, imprisoned for years after the revolution.

## Timeline

1840: Sultan Seyyid Said makes Zanzibar the main capital of his empire.
1873: The slave market is closed by treaty.
1890: Zanzibar becomes a British protectorate.
27 August 1896: The Anglo-Zanzibar War, lasting less than an hour.
1957: First general election in Zanzibar.
June 1961: Election riots kill dozens of people.
July 1963: The ASP wins most votes, but the ZNP–ZPPP coalition forms the government.
10 December 1963: Independence under Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah.
12 January 1964: The revolution; the Sultan flees.
26 April 1964: Zanzibar unites with Tanganyika.
7 April 1972: Abeid Karume is assassinated.
1992: Multi-party politics returns.
2010: A referendum approves a Government of National Unity.

## Sources

Abdul Sheriff and Ed Ferguson (eds.), Zanzibar Under Colonial Rule (1991). Jonathon Glassman, War of Words, War of Stones (2011). Anthony Clayton, The Zanzibar Revolution and Its Aftermath (1981). G. Thomas Burgess, Race, Revolution, and the Struggle for Human Rights in Zanzibar (2009).

en.title: TANU: the party that won Tanganyika's freedom
en.text:
## Seven July 1954

On 7 July 1954, seventeen men met in a small building on Lumumba Street in Dar es Salaam. They agreed to transform the Tanganyika African Association, a mostly social club of civil servants and teachers, into a political party: the Tanganyika African National Union, TANU. They elected as president a quiet 32-year-old teacher, Julius Kambarage Nyerere.

Seven years later Tanganyika was independent. The date, Saba Saba, seven seven, is still remembered in Tanzania.

## Tanganyika under British trusteeship

After Germany lost the First World War, Britain governed Tanganyika under a League of Nations mandate, and from 1946 as a United Nations trust territory. That status meant Britain was supposed to prepare the country for self-government, and the UN sent visiting missions every three years. Tanganyikans could send petitions to the UN.

But in practice, power was in British hands, with a large say for the small European settler and Asian communities. Africans, the vast majority, had little voice. British officials often imagined that self-government would take many decades.

## From association to party

The Tanganyika African Association had been founded in 1929. After the Second World War, educated Africans, returning soldiers and urban workers grew more political. Nyerere, back from studying at Edinburgh University, was elected president of the TAA in 1953 and pushed to turn it into a true national movement.

TANU's first constitution set clear aims: to prepare the people for self-government and independence, to fight tribalism and all forms of racial discrimination, and to build a democratic government with an African majority.

## Building from the ground

TANU's strength was organisation. It sold membership cards for a small fee, and members joined branches in towns and villages. The party grew from a few hundred members to hundreds of thousands within a few years.

Leaders travelled the country by bus, train, bicycle and on foot. Nyerere himself gave up his teaching job at Pugu in 1955 to work full-time for the party.

Women were central. Bibi Titi Mohammed, a singer and community leader from Dar es Salaam, joined in 1955 and built TANU's women's section, recruiting thousands of women within months. Women sang political songs, organised meetings and raised funds. Their support was a key reason TANU became a truly mass movement.

Kiswahili was TANU's language. Speeches, songs and newspapers in a shared language helped people from more than 120 ethnic groups feel part of one national struggle.

## Speaking to the world

In 1955 Nyerere travelled to New York to speak to the UN Trusteeship Council. Calm, reasonable and determined, he argued that Tanganyika should be guided toward African majority government, and he asked for a timetable. His appearance raised TANU's profile internationally and showed that its leaders were ready to govern.

## The colonial response

Governor Sir Edward Twining distrusted TANU. The government banned some branches, prevented civil servants from joining, and backed a rival multiracial party, the United Tanganyika Party. Nyerere was taken to court for libel in 1958 after writing about corrupt officials, and fined.

The government also designed a complicated voting system for the 1958–59 elections: every voter had to vote for three candidates, one African, one Asian and one European, in each constituency. Some in TANU wanted to boycott. At a conference in Tabora in 1958, Nyerere persuaded the party to take part, and to back sympathetic Asian and European candidates.

## Victory

The strategy worked. TANU and its allies won every seat they contested in 1958–59. The new governor, Sir Richard Turnbull, chose to cooperate with Nyerere. In the 1960 elections TANU won 70 of the 71 seats. Nyerere became chief minister, then prime minister when internal self-government came in May 1961. On 9 December 1961, Tanganyika became independent.

Unlike Kenya, Algeria or Mozambique, Tanganyika won its independence without armed struggle. Historians give credit to TANU's discipline and unity, Nyerere's leadership, the trusteeship system, and a British government that by then accepted decolonisation.

## After independence

TANU became the governing party. In 1965 Tanzania became a one-party state, an arrangement Nyerere defended as better suited to building national unity, though critics saw it as limiting freedom. TANU's ideas were set out in the Arusha Declaration of 1967.

On 5 February 1977, TANU merged with Zanzibar's Afro-Shirazi Party to form Chama Cha Mapinduzi, CCM, which has governed Tanzania ever since. Multi-party politics returned in 1992.

## Remembering Saba Saba

The building where TANU was founded is now a museum. The Dar es Salaam International Trade Fair is held every year around 7 July, and Saba Saba is a public holiday. TANU's motto, "Uhuru na Umoja", Freedom and Unity, is still the national motto of Tanzania.

## Founders and supporters

TANU's founders included teachers, civil servants and businessmen from Dar es Salaam. Brothers Abdulwahid and Ally Sykes, from a prominent family in the city, had been leaders of the Tanganyika African Association and played a key role in the transition to TANU. Businessmen such as John Rupia helped fund the young party. Many early members were Muslims from the coastal towns, and Islamic associations and networks helped spread TANU's message.

## Farmers and cooperatives

Rural Tanganyika was the heart of the country, and TANU's success depended on farmers. In the Lake Province, cotton growers in Sukumaland had their own grievances against colonial agricultural rules, such as forced soil conservation measures. Cooperative leaders like Paul Bomani built powerful farmers' organisations, and these networks joined forces with TANU. On Kilimanjaro, coffee growers' cooperatives were also politically active.

Colonial rules about cattle, land and farming methods, imposed without consultation, angered many rural people. TANU gave that anger a peaceful, national direction.

## Discipline and non-violence

From the beginning Nyerere insisted on non-violence and discipline. TANU members were told not to break the law or respond to provocation, so that the colonial government would have no excuse to ban the party entirely. This strategy contrasted with the violence of the Mau Mau war in neighbouring Kenya at the same time, and helped convince British officials that TANU was a responsible partner.

## Spreading the word

TANU used newspapers, pamphlets and above all public meetings. Songs composed for the movement spread from region to region. The party's youth league organised volunteers. Party cards became prized possessions, and in many villages holding a TANU card was a sign of commitment to the future.

## Lessons of TANU

Historians see TANU as one of the most successful nationalist movements in Africa. It combined a clear goal, a single national language, a message that rejected tribalism and racism, strong organisation from village to capital, and leaders who knew how to use international pressure. Many of those qualities shaped the peaceful, united character of independent Tanzania.

## Bibi Titi Mohammed

Bibi Titi Mohammed, born in Dar es Salaam in 1926, was a popular singer in a women's music group before she joined TANU in 1955. Nyerere and other leaders quickly saw her gift for speaking to crowds. She became head of the TANU women's section and travelled the country recruiting women, who joined in huge numbers. Many historians argue that without the women she organised, TANU could not have grown so quickly.

After independence she became a member of parliament and a junior minister. Her later life was tragic: in 1970 she was convicted in a treason trial and imprisoned, then pardoned in 1972. In her final years she was honoured again, and a major street in Dar es Salaam bears her name. Her story shows both the central role of women in the independence struggle and the hard politics that followed.

## The voice at the United Nations

When Nyerere spoke to the UN Trusteeship Council in 1955, he made a careful case. He did not attack Britain angrily. Instead he pointed out that Tanganyika was a trust territory, that the purpose of trusteeship was self-government, and that the African majority must be the basis of any future government. He asked Britain to declare that Tanganyika would become an African state.

His moderate tone surprised many observers and won respect. Back home, his reports of the visit to New York helped TANU members feel that the world was listening.

## Key people

Julius Nyerere: founding president of TANU.
Bibi Titi Mohammed: leader of the women's section.
Abdulwahid and Ally Sykes: Dar es Salaam leaders of the TAA and TANU's early years.
Rashidi Kawawa: trade union leader who brought organised workers into the movement.
Oscar Kambona: TANU secretary-general.
Paul Bomani: cooperative leader from the Lake region who linked farmers to TANU.

## Timeline

1929: The Tanganyika African Association (TAA) is founded.
1953: Julius Nyerere is elected president of the TAA.
7 July 1954: TANU is founded in Dar es Salaam.
1955: Bibi Titi Mohammed joins and builds the women's section; Nyerere speaks at the UN and leaves teaching.
1958: The Tabora conference decides to take part in the elections.
1958–1959: TANU-backed candidates win every seat they contest.
1960: TANU wins 70 of 71 seats.
9 December 1961: Independence.
1965: Tanzania becomes a one-party state.
5 February 1967: TANU adopts the Arusha Declaration.
5 February 1977: TANU merges with the Afro-Shirazi Party to form CCM.

## Sources

John Iliffe, A Modern History of Tanganyika (1979). Susan Geiger, TANU Women (1997). Julius Nyerere, Freedom and Unity (1967).

en.title: Mwalimu Julius Nyerere: the teacher who built a nation
en.place: Butiama, Dar es Salaam and London
en.text:
## A death that stopped a nation

On 14 October 1999, Julius Kambarage Nyerere died of leukaemia at St Thomas' Hospital in London, aged 77. In Tanzania, radios fell silent and people wept in the streets. Across Africa and beyond, leaders paid tribute to one of the most respected figures of the twentieth century. Tanzanians knew him simply as Mwalimu, the Teacher.

## Childhood in Butiama

Nyerere was born in 1922 in Butiama, a village near Lake Victoria in what is now the Mara region. His father, Nyerere Burito, was a chief of the small Zanaki people, and had many wives. Julius's mother was Mugaya Nyang'ombe.

As a boy he herded cattle. He began school relatively late, at about twelve, walking long distances to Musoma. He was so able that he moved quickly to the Government School at Tabora, one of the best schools for Africans in the territory, where he was known as a gifted student and debater. He became a Catholic while studying.

## Teacher and scholar

Nyerere studied at Makerere College in Uganda, the leading university college of East Africa, gaining a diploma in education. He then taught at St Mary's School in Tabora.

In 1949 he won a scholarship to the University of Edinburgh in Scotland, becoming one of the first Tanganyikans to study at a British university. He earned a Master of Arts in history and political economy in 1952. In Britain he read widely about socialism, democracy and colonialism, and met other African students.

He returned home, married Maria Gabriel Magige, and taught history at St Francis' College, Pugu, near Dar es Salaam.

## Leader of the struggle

In 1953 Nyerere was elected president of the Tanganyika African Association, and in 1954 he founded TANU. He gave up his teaching job in 1955 to lead the independence movement full-time.

He built TANU on peaceful, disciplined methods and a message of unity across ethnic groups and races. He argued Tanganyika's case at the UN in New York. Under his leadership TANU won the elections of 1958 to 1960, and on 9 December 1961 Tanganyika became independent with Nyerere as prime minister. In 1962 he became the first president of the republic, and in 1964 he led the union with Zanzibar to form Tanzania.

## Ujamaa and the Arusha Declaration

Nyerere believed that African society had traditions of sharing and community that could be the basis of a modern, fair nation. He called this Ujamaa, "family-hood", a form of African socialism.

On 5 February 1967 TANU adopted the Arusha Declaration. It nationalised banks, major industries and large plantations, and set out the goals of self-reliance, equality, and a ban on leaders accumulating private wealth.

From 1973 to 1976, the government moved millions of rural people into planned Ujamaa villages, where services could be provided more easily and farming could be collective. Many moved willingly, but in Operation Vijiji many were forced, sometimes violently, and some villages were placed on poor land.

## Achievements and failures

The record is mixed, and Nyerere himself said so.

Achievements: Tanzania became one of the most peaceful and united countries in Africa. Kiswahili became a strong national language. Primary education became nearly universal, adult literacy campaigns were among the most successful in the world, and clinics and clean water reached many villages. Ethnic division was strongly discouraged.

Failures: collective farming largely failed, state-run industries were inefficient, and by the late 1970s and early 1980s the economy was in crisis, with shortages of basic goods. The one-party state, created in 1965, limited political freedom, and people were detained without trial under preventive detention laws. Nyerere admitted publicly that mistakes had been made.

## Africa's champion

Abroad, Nyerere was a towering figure. Dar es Salaam hosted the OAU Liberation Committee and gave bases, training and refuge to liberation movements from Mozambique, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Namibia and Angola, at great cost to Tanzania. He was a leader of the Front Line States against white minority rule.

In 1978 Idi Amin's Uganda invaded north-western Tanzania. Tanzania counter-attacked, and in April 1979 Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles captured Kampala and ended Amin's brutal rule.

## Stepping down

In 1985 Nyerere did something rare among African leaders of his time: he voluntarily stepped down as president, handing over to Ali Hassan Mwinyi. He remained chairman of CCM until 1990 and supported the return of multi-party politics in 1992. In his last years he worked as a mediator in the Burundi peace process.

## The man

Nyerere lived simply and was widely regarded as incorruptible. He loved books and learning, and translated Shakespeare's Julius Caesar and The Merchant of Venice into Kiswahili. He wrote many books on politics and society, including Freedom and Unity and Ujamaa: Essays on Socialism.

He was buried in Butiama, where his home is now a museum. In 2005 the Catholic Church began the process that could one day lead to his beatification, giving him the title Servant of God.

## Legacy

Nyerere Day, 14 October, is a public holiday. The country's largest national park and many institutions bear his name. Debates about his economic policies continue, but his commitment to unity, equality, education and African liberation remains a guiding example for many Tanzanians and Africans.

## Education for self-reliance

Nyerere, a teacher by profession, believed education should serve the whole community, not just produce a small elite. In 1967 he wrote "Education for Self-Reliance", arguing that schools should teach practical skills, link learning to farming and community work, and value cooperation over competition.

Under his government, primary schooling expanded rapidly, and in the 1970s Tanzania declared universal primary education. Adult education campaigns taught millions of adults to read and write, often in village classes held under trees, using radio programmes and simple booklets in Kiswahili.

## Tanzania and the world

Nyerere followed a policy of non-alignment, refusing to join either side in the Cold War. He accepted help from the West, China and the Soviet bloc, but on Tanzania's terms. When Western countries refused to finance a railway linking landlocked Zambia to the sea, avoiding white-ruled Rhodesia and South Africa, China agreed. The Tanzania-Zambia Railway, TAZARA, built between 1970 and 1975, became one of the largest foreign aid projects of its time.

Nyerere was not afraid to take costly stands. In 1965 Tanzania broke diplomatic relations with Britain over its failure to act against the white minority regime in Rhodesia, even though this meant losing British aid.

## Family and personal life

Nyerere married Maria Gabriel Magige in 1953. Maria Nyerere was a teacher too, and supported him throughout his political life; she lived quietly in Butiama after his death. The couple had several children. Nyerere was known for avoiding the luxury that many leaders enjoyed, preferring a modest house and simple food.

## His words

Nyerere was a gifted speaker and writer in both Kiswahili and English. He often spoke about human equality, the dignity of work, and the duty of the educated to serve those who paid for their education. His speeches and essays are still read in schools and universities across Africa.

## Remembering Mwalimu

At his funeral in 1999, leaders from across Africa and the world came to Dar es Salaam. His body lay in state as hundreds of thousands of people filed past. He was then flown home and buried in the family graveyard at Butiama. The Mwalimu Nyerere Museum in Butiama and the Mwalimu Nyerere Foundation continue to preserve his papers and promote his ideas.

## Critics and admirers

Nyerere's admirers point to peace, unity, literacy, a strong national language and his principled support for African liberation. Many see him as one of the few African leaders of his era who did not enrich himself and who handed over power peacefully.

His critics point to the failure of collective agriculture, the economic crisis of the late 1970s and early 1980s, forced villagisation, and the detention of political opponents under the one-party state. Some economists argue that his policies made Tanzania poorer than it needed to be.

Nyerere himself reflected on these questions in his later years, admitting failures while defending his goals of equality and self-reliance. That honesty is itself part of why he is respected.

## Timeline

1922: Born in Butiama, near Lake Victoria.
1945: Completes a teaching diploma at Makerere College, Uganda.
1949–1952: Studies at the University of Edinburgh, earning an MA.
1953: Marries Maria Gabriel Magige; elected president of the TAA.
1954: Founds TANU.
1961: Becomes prime minister at independence.
1962: Becomes the first president of the Republic of Tanganyika.
1964: Leads the union with Zanzibar to form Tanzania.
1967: The Arusha Declaration and "Education for Self-Reliance".
1970–1975: The TAZARA railway is built with Chinese support.
1978–1979: War with Idi Amin's Uganda.
1985: Steps down as president.
1990: Steps down as chairman of CCM.
14 October 1999: Dies in London; buried in Butiama.

## Sources

Julius Nyerere, Freedom and Unity (1967) and Ujamaa: Essays on Socialism (1968). Issa Shivji, Saida Yahya-Othman and Ng'wanza Kamata, Development as Rebellion: A Biography of Julius Nyerere (2020). John Iliffe, A Modern History of Tanganyika (1979).

en.title: The summit of Kilimanjaro is reached
en.text:
On 6 October 1889, three men stood on the highest point of Kilimanjaro, the roof of Africa, after a long climb across ice. They were the German geologist Hans Meyer, the Austrian mountaineer Ludwig Purtscheller, and their local guide from Marangu, Yohani Kinyala Lauwo.

Kilimanjaro rises 5,895 metres above sea level. It is the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain on Earth. It is a huge volcano with three cones: Kibo, the highest; jagged Mawenzi; and the old, worn Shira plateau.

For the Chagga people living on its fertile slopes, the mountain was home, a source of water and a place woven into their stories. Europeans long refused to believe reports, first written in 1848 by the missionary Johannes Rebmann, of a snow-covered mountain so near the equator.

Meyer had failed on two earlier attempts. In 1889 the team climbed with porters and Lauwo's guidance, setting up camps on the way. On the summit Meyer named the highest point Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze after the German emperor. Lauwo, who was still in his teens at the time, went on to guide climbers for decades; Tanzania later honoured his role.

At independence in 1961 the summit was renamed Uhuru Peak, Freedom Peak, and the Uhuru Torch was lit there.

Today more than 30,000 people try to climb Kilimanjaro each year, most guided and supported by Tanzanian guides and porters. Its famous glaciers, however, are shrinking quickly. Scientists warn that most of the ice that has crowned the mountain for thousands of years could disappear within decades.

fr.title: Le sommet du Kilimandjaro est atteint
fr.text: Hans Meyer et Ludwig Purtscheller atteignent le sommet Kibo du Kilimandjaro, la plus haute montagne d'Afrique. C'est la première ascension du sommet attestée.

ar.title: الوصول إلى قمة كليمنجارو
ar.text: وصل هانز ماير ولودفيغ بورتشيلر إلى قمة كيبو في جبل كليمنجارو، أعلى جبل في أفريقيا. وكان ذلك أول صعود مسجَّل إلى القمة.

ko.title: 킬리만자로 정상 등정
ko.text: 한스 마이어와 루트비히 푸르첼러가 아프리카 최고봉인 킬리만자로산의 키보 정상에 올랐습니다. 이는 기록으로 남은 최초의 정상 등정이었습니다.

es.text: Hans Meyer y Ludwig Purtscheller llegaron a la cima Kibo del Kilimanjaro, la montaña más alta de África. Fue el primer ascenso registrado a la cumbre.

sw.text: Hans Meyer na Ludwig Purtscheller walifika kilele cha Kibo cha Mlima Kilimanjaro, mlima mrefu zaidi barani Afrika. Ni mara ya kwanza iliyorekodiwa kwa wapandaji kufika kileleni.

en.title: The Organisation of African Unity is founded
en.text:
On 25 May 1963, leaders of 32 independent African states gathered in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, and signed the charter of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU). It was the first organisation to bring almost the whole of independent Africa together.

The meeting was hosted by Emperor Haile Selassie. It included leaders such as Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, Julius Nyerere of Tanganyika, Sékou Touré of Guinea, Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt and Modibo Keïta of Mali.

The leaders disagreed about how far unity should go. Nkrumah wanted a full union of African states with one government. Others preferred cooperation between sovereign countries. The OAU took the second path, but it agreed on shared goals: defend independence, improve life for Africans, and free the continent from colonialism and apartheid.

The OAU's Liberation Committee was based in Dar es Salaam. It channelled money, training and support to liberation movements fighting in Mozambique, Angola, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Guinea-Bissau and South Africa.

The OAU also accepted the borders left by colonial powers, to avoid endless wars over territory, and insisted on non-interference in members' internal affairs. Critics later said this let some governments abuse their people without challenge.

In 2002 the OAU was replaced by the African Union, which has stronger powers to act in crises. The founding date, 25 May, is celebrated each year as Africa Day across the continent and among Africans around the world.

fr.text: Les dirigeants des États africains indépendants fondent l'OUA, ancêtre de l'Union africaine (UA). Cette date est aujourd'hui célébrée comme la Journée de l'Afrique.

en.title: Nelson Mandela is released
en.place: Paarl and Cape Town, South Africa
en.text:
On the afternoon of 11 February 1990, Nelson Mandela walked out of the gates of Victor Verster Prison near Paarl, holding hands with his wife Winnie, and raised his fist. He had been in prison for 27 years. Television carried the moment to the whole world.

Mandela, born in 1918 in the Eastern Cape, was a lawyer and a leader of the African National Congress (ANC). He fought apartheid, the system of laws that separated South Africans by race and denied the Black majority the vote, good land, and freedom of movement.

After the ANC was banned in 1960, Mandela helped form its armed wing. Arrested in 1962, he was tried with other leaders in the Rivonia Trial. In 1964 he told the court that a democratic, free society was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. He was sentenced to life imprisonment.

He spent 18 years on Robben Island, breaking rocks in a lime quarry, then years in other prisons. His name became a worldwide symbol, and campaigns, boycotts and sanctions pressured the apartheid government.

On 2 February 1990, President F. W. de Klerk announced the unbanning of the ANC and other movements. Nine days later Mandela was free. That evening he spoke from the balcony of Cape Town City Hall to a huge crowd, calling for continued struggle and for peace.

Negotiations followed, through years of violence. In April 1994 South Africa held its first election in which all citizens could vote, and Mandela became president. He and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. Mandela died in 2013, honoured as one of the great peacemakers of history.

fr.title: Nelson Mandela est libéré
fr.text: Nelson Mandela est libéré après 27 ans de prison. Quatre ans plus tard, il devient le premier président de l'Afrique du Sud élu lors d'une élection pleinement démocratique.

es.title: Nelson Mandela es liberado
es.text: Nelson Mandela fue liberado tras 27 años en prisión. Cuatro años después se convirtió en el primer presidente de Sudáfrica elegido en unas elecciones plenamente democráticas.

sw.title: Nelson Mandela aachiliwa huru

en.title: Ghana gains independence
en.text:
At midnight on 6 March 1957, at the Old Polo Grounds in Accra, Kwame Nkrumah stood before a cheering crowd and declared that Ghana was free forever. The British colony of the Gold Coast became Ghana, one of the first countries in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from colonial rule.

The name Ghana was chosen on purpose. It recalled the ancient empire of Ghana, or Wagadu, a rich West African kingdom known for gold, which flourished more than a thousand years earlier, to the north-west of the modern country.

The Gold Coast had been ruled by Britain since the nineteenth century, after long resistance including the Anglo-Asante wars. After the Second World War, returning soldiers, farmers angry about low cocoa prices, and educated young people demanded change. Riots in 1948 shook the colonial government.

Nkrumah, who had studied in the United States and Britain, founded the Convention People's Party in 1949 and called for "self-government now". He was jailed for organising strikes, but his party won elections while he was in prison, and he was released to lead the government.

In his independence speech, Nkrumah said that Ghana's freedom would be meaningless unless it was linked to the total liberation of Africa. Ghana's black star flag became a symbol for the whole continent, and Accra hosted meetings of African liberation movements.

Nkrumah was overthrown in a coup in 1966 and Ghana went through difficult decades. Since 1992 it has held regular democratic elections. 6 March remains Ghana's Independence Day, and the date is seen as the moment a wave of African independence began.

fr.title: Le Ghana obtient son indépendance
fr.text: Le Ghana, dirigé par Kwame Nkrumah, obtient son indépendance du Royaume-Uni et devient un exemple pour les mouvements d'indépendance de toute l'Afrique.

ar.title: غانا تنال استقلالها
ar.text: نالت غانا، بقيادة كوامي نكروما، استقلالها عن بريطانيا، وأصبحت قدوة لحركات الاستقلال في جميع أنحاء أفريقيا.

ko.title: 가나 독립

ja.title: ガーナが独立
ja.text: クワメ・エンクルマ率いるガーナがイギリスから独立し、アフリカ各地の独立運動の模範となりました。

zh.title: 加纳独立
zh.text: 在克瓦米·恩克鲁玛的领导下,加纳脱离英国获得独立,成为整个非洲独立运动的榜样。

es.title: Ghana obtiene su independencia
es.text: Ghana, liderada por Kwame Nkrumah, obtuvo su independencia del Reino Unido y se convirtió en un ejemplo para los movimientos de independencia de toda África.

sw.title: Ghana yapata uhuru
sw.text: Ghana, chini ya uongozi wa Kwame Nkrumah, ilipata uhuru kutoka kwa Uingereza na kuwa mfano kwa harakati za uhuru kote barani Afrika.

en.title: Humans walk on the Moon
en.text:
On 20 July 1969, the lunar module Eagle landed on a flat plain on the Moon called the Sea of Tranquillity. Hours later, Neil Armstrong climbed down the ladder and became the first human being to step onto another world.

Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July on a giant Saturn V rocket. On board were three American astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Collins stayed in orbit in the command module Columbia while Armstrong and Aldrin flew Eagle down to the surface.

The landing was dangerous. Computer alarms sounded, and the planned site was full of boulders, so Armstrong flew on by hand and landed with very little fuel left. His first words from the surface were that Tranquility Base was here and the Eagle had landed.

Armstrong and Aldrin spent about two and a half hours walking outside. They planted a flag, set up experiments including a laser reflector and a seismometer, and collected 21.5 kilograms of rocks and soil. An estimated 600 million people watched on television, one of the largest audiences in history.

The mission was the high point of the space race between the United States and the Soviet Union, which had already sent the first satellite and the first human into space. Thousands of engineers, scientists and mathematicians worked on Apollo, including Black women mathematicians such as Katherine Johnson, whose calculations were crucial to the programme.

The crew returned safely on 24 July. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon. No one has returned since, but new missions plan to take humans back.

fr.title: L'homme marche sur la Lune
fr.text: Neil Armstrong et Buzz Aldrin, de la mission Apollo 11, deviennent les premiers êtres humains à marcher sur la Lune, tandis que Michael Collins reste en orbite dans le module de commande.

ar.title: الإنسان يمشي على القمر
ar.text: أصبح نيل أرمسترونغ وباز ألدرين من مهمة أبولو 11 أول إنسانين يمشيان على سطح القمر، بينما كان مايكل كولينز يدور حول القمر في وحدة القيادة.

ko.title: 인류, 달에 발을 딛다
ko.text: 아폴로 11호의 닐 암스트롱과 버즈 올드린이 달 위를 걸은 최초의 인류가 되었고, 마이클 콜린스는 사령선을 타고 달 궤도를 돌았습니다.

ja.title: 人類が月面を歩く
ja.text: アポロ11号のニール・アームストロングとバズ・オルドリンが月面を歩いた最初の人類となり、マイケル・コリンズは司令船で月の周回軌道を回りました。

zh.title: 人类登上月球
zh.text: 阿波罗11号的尼尔·阿姆斯特朗和巴兹·奥尔德林成为首批在月球上行走的人类,迈克尔·柯林斯则驾驶指令舱环绕月球飞行。

es.title: El ser humano pisa la Luna

en.title: The first human in space
en.text:
On the morning of 12 April 1961, a 27-year-old Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin lay strapped inside a small round capsule called Vostok 1. As the rocket lifted off from Baikonur, in today's Kazakhstan, he called out "Poyekhali!", "Let's go!" He was about to become the first human being in space.

Gagarin was the son of a carpenter and a dairy worker from a village west of Moscow. He trained as a foundry worker, joined a flying club, and became a fighter pilot. Out of thousands of candidates, he was chosen partly for his calm nature and his small size, which suited the cramped capsule.

The flight lasted 108 minutes. Gagarin circled the Earth once, travelling at about 27,000 kilometres per hour. He reported what he saw: the curve of the planet, the blue band of the atmosphere, the darkness of space. The capsule was controlled from the ground, since no one yet knew how a human would cope with weightlessness.

On the way down, at about seven kilometres above the ground, Gagarin ejected from the capsule as planned and landed by parachute in a field near the Volga River. A farmer and her granddaughter were the first people to meet him.

His flight shocked the United States and sped up the space race, leading President Kennedy to set the goal of reaching the Moon. Gagarin became a hero across the world, visiting many countries.

He died in 1968 in a training jet crash. 12 April is now celebrated by the United Nations as the International Day of Human Space Flight.

en.title: The first World Cup final
en.text:
On 30 July 1930, in the brand-new Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2 to win the first ever FIFA World Cup. Around 68,000 people watched in the stadium, and the next day was declared a national holiday in Uruguay.

The tournament was the dream of Jules Rimet, the French president of FIFA. Football had been played at the Olympic Games, and Uruguay had won the Olympic title in 1924 and 1928. In 1930 Uruguay was also celebrating 100 years of its first constitution, so it was chosen as host and promised to pay travel costs for visiting teams.

Even so, only 13 teams took part. Travelling from Europe meant weeks at sea, and only four European nations made the journey: France, Belgium, Romania and Yugoslavia. Some of them sailed together on the same ship, the SS Conte Verde.

The first ever World Cup goal was scored by Lucien Laurent of France against Mexico on 13 July. The Estadio Centenario was not finished in time for the opening games because of heavy rain during construction.

The final was a fierce rivalry between neighbours. Each team wanted to use its own ball, so the first half was played with Argentina's ball and the second with Uruguay's. Argentina led 2–1 at half-time, but Uruguay scored three times in the second half.

From those small beginnings, the World Cup became the most watched sporting event on Earth. The 2026 tournament in North America is the first with 48 teams.

en.title: The World Cup comes to Africa
en.text:
On 11 June 2010, the FIFA World Cup kicked off for the first time on African soil. In Soccer City stadium in Johannesburg, the hosts South Africa played Mexico. When Siphiwe Tshabalala struck a beautiful goal for South Africa, the noise of tens of thousands of vuvuzelas filled the stadium. The match ended 1–1.

Africa had waited 80 years. African teams had long complained that the continent was overlooked, and South Africa had narrowly lost the vote for the 2006 tournament. In 2004 FIFA chose South Africa to host in 2010, only ten years after the end of apartheid.

Nelson Mandela, then 91, had campaigned for the bid. His presence at the final, waving to the crowd from a small cart, was one of the most emotional moments of the tournament.

The country built and upgraded stadiums, roads, airports and rail lines, including the Gautrain. Critics argued that the money could have been spent on housing and services, and that some stadiums would be little used afterwards, a debate that still continues.

On the field, South Africa became the first host nation to go out in the group stage, though it beat France. Ghana carried Africa's hopes into the quarter-finals, where they lost to Uruguay on penalties after a last-minute handball on the goal line denied them a winning goal.

Spain won the final against the Netherlands 1–0 with a goal by Andrés Iniesta. The tournament showed the world a confident, welcoming Africa and remains a source of pride across the continent.

en.title: Filbert Bayi sets a world record
en.text:
On 2 February 1974, at the Commonwealth Games in Christchurch, New Zealand, a 20-year-old Tanzanian runner named Filbert Bayi did something experts said was impossible. He led the 1,500 metres from the very first stride, and kept running away from the world's best.

Most middle-distance races of the time were tactical: runners stayed together and sprinted at the end. Bayi ran differently. He went straight to the front and set a fierce pace, daring the others to keep up.

Behind him was a brilliant field, including New Zealand's John Walker and Kenya's Ben Jipcho. Walker closed in on the final straight, but Bayi held on. He crossed the line in 3 minutes 32.16 seconds, breaking the world record held for seven years by the American Jim Ryun. Walker, second, also ran under the old record. It is still remembered as one of the greatest 1,500-metre races ever run.

Bayi was born in 1953 near Karatu in northern Tanzania, and grew up running long distances at high altitude. He trained while serving in the Tanzania People's Defence Force.

In 1975 he broke the world record for the mile as well, running 3 minutes 51.0 seconds in Jamaica. Tanzania's boycott of the 1976 Montreal Olympics, in protest against apartheid sport links, kept him from a showdown there. In 1980 in Moscow he won Olympic silver in the 3,000-metre steeplechase.

Later he founded the Filbert Bayi Foundation and schools in Tanzania to support young athletes. His race in Christchurch remains a proud moment in Tanzanian and African sporting history.

fr.text: Le coureur tanzanien Filbert Bayi remporte le 1 500 mètres aux Jeux du Commonwealth et établit un nouveau record du monde, en menant la course du début à la fin.

en.title: The Titanic sinks
en.text:
At 11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912, lookouts on the RMS Titanic saw an iceberg directly ahead. The ship turned, but too late. The iceberg scraped along the starboard side, opening several watertight compartments to the sea. In less than three hours, the largest ship in the world was gone.

Titanic was on her maiden voyage from Southampton in England to New York, with stops in France and Ireland. She was a symbol of wealth and modern engineering. About 2,224 people were on board, from millionaires in luxury suites to emigrants in third class hoping for a new life in America.

The ship carried lifeboats for only about 1,178 people, which was within the law of the time. Crew members were not fully trained to launch them, and many early boats left half empty. Third-class passengers, deep in the ship, had the hardest path to the boat deck.

At 2:20 a.m. on 15 April the ship broke apart and sank. More than 1,500 people died, most of them in the freezing water. The liner Carpathia, racing through the ice after hearing distress signals, rescued about 705 survivors later that morning.

The disaster led to the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea in 1914. Ships were required to carry enough lifeboats for everyone, keep radio watch 24 hours a day, and the International Ice Patrol was created.

The wreck was found in 1985, about 3,800 metres deep, by a team led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel. Today it is protected as a memorial site.
