en.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza is built
en.text:
Around 2560 BCE, workers in ancient Egypt completed the largest pyramid ever built, on the plateau of Giza beside the Nile. It was the tomb of Pharaoh Khufu, a king of the Fourth Dynasty. Today it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

The pyramid was originally about 146 metres tall. For around 3,800 years it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth. It contains roughly 2.3 million blocks of stone, most of them limestone, some weighing several tonnes, with granite beams in the King's Chamber brought from Aswan, about 800 kilometres up the Nile.

It was once covered with polished white limestone casing stones that shone in the sun. Most of these were removed in later centuries and reused in buildings in Cairo.

For a long time people believed the pyramids were built by slaves. Archaeologists now know that the builders were organised teams of paid workers and skilled craftsmen. Near Giza they found a workers' town with bakeries, breweries, and cemeteries where workers were buried with honour.

In 2013, papyri were discovered at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast. They include the logbook of an official named Merer, who described moving limestone blocks by boat along canals from the Tura quarries to Giza. They are the oldest inscribed papyri ever found.

Exactly how the stones were raised is still debated: ramps, levers and great skill all played a role. The Great Pyramid is aligned almost perfectly to the four compass points, a sign of the astronomy and mathematics of its builders.

sw.title: Piramidi Kuu ya Giza yajengwa
sw.text: Wafanyakazi wa Misri ya kale walikamilisha Piramidi Kuu ya Giza kama kaburi la Farao Khufu. Kwa zaidi ya miaka 3,800 ilikuwa jengo refu zaidi lililowahi kujengwa na binadamu.

en.title: Mansa Musa's journey to Mecca
en.place: Mali Empire to Cairo and Mecca
en.text:
In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, set out on the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. His journey across the Sahara and through Cairo became one of the most famous travels of the Middle Ages, and made the wealth of West Africa known across the world.

Mali was founded in the 1230s by Sundiata Keita. By Musa's time it stretched from the Atlantic coast deep into the interior, controlling trade routes and the goldfields of Bambuk and Bure. Much of the gold used in North Africa and Europe came from West Africa.

Writers described a vast caravan, with thousands of people and camels carrying gold. When Musa reached Cairo, he and his followers spent and gave away so much gold that, according to the historian al-Umari who visited Cairo years later, the value of gold there was still lower than before.

Musa returned with scholars and architects, among them the Andalusian poet and architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. Under Musa, Timbuktu grew into a great centre of learning and trade. The Djinguereber Mosque there, built in his time, still stands.

Europe took notice. On the Catalan Atlas, made in 1375 in Majorca, Mansa Musa is painted sitting on a throne in West Africa, wearing a crown and holding a large gold nugget.

The Mali Empire declined in the fifteenth century and was overtaken by the Songhai Empire. But Mansa Musa's hajj remains a symbol of the wealth, faith and learning of medieval African kingdoms.

sw.title: Safari ya Mansa Musa kwenda Makka
sw.text: Mansa Musa, mtawala wa Dola ya Mali, alisafiri kwenda Makka akiwa na msafara mkubwa uliobeba dhahabu nyingi, kiasi kwamba safari yake ilijulikana kote Afrika, Mashariki ya Kati na Ulaya.

en.title: Kilwa Kisiwani: the golden age of a Swahili city
en.text:
## An island of stone

On a small island off the southern coast of Tanzania stand the ruins of a city that was once one of the richest in Africa. Kilwa Kisiwani, "Kilwa on the island", controlled much of the gold trade of the western Indian Ocean in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its coral-stone mosques, palaces and houses amazed visitors from across the Islamic world.

## Who built Kilwa

A famous chronicle of Kilwa, written down in the sixteenth century, tells that the city was founded by Ali ibn al-Hasan, a prince from Shiraz in Persia, who bought the island from a local ruler for a quantity of cloth. This "Shirazi" founding story was important to Kilwa's rulers, giving them prestigious foreign ancestry.

Archaeology tells a more African story. People were living on the island and trading by the ninth century, long before any Persian prince. The Swahili people of the coast were African communities, speaking a Bantu language, who over centuries became deeply connected to the Indian Ocean world through trade, Islam and marriage. Their language, Kiswahili, borrowed many words from Arabic, but its grammar and roots are African.

## The source of the wealth: gold

Kilwa's fortune came from gold. Far to the south, in the kingdoms of the Zimbabwe plateau, centred on Great Zimbabwe, gold was mined and carried to the coastal town of Sofala in present-day Mozambique.

Kilwa took control of Sofala, and with it the gold trade. Merchants arrived from Arabia, Persia and India on the monsoon winds, which blow from the north-east in one season and from the south-west in the other. They brought cotton cloth, glass beads, Chinese porcelain and Persian pottery. They left with gold, ivory, tortoiseshell, timber and other African goods.

Kilwa minted its own copper coins, one of very few places in sub-Saharan Africa to do so. One Kilwa coin was found in the 1940s on an island in northern Australia, and others have turned up across the region, a sign of how far its trade reached.

## The golden age

In the late thirteenth century a new dynasty, the Mahdali, came to power. Under them Kilwa reached its height. The most famous of these sultans was al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman, who ruled in the early fourteenth century and was known as Abu al-Mawahib, "the father of gifts".

He built Husuni Kubwa, a vast palace on a cliff above the sea. It had more than a hundred rooms, courtyards, a sunken bathing pool and a great audience court. It was one of the largest buildings in sub-Saharan Africa of its time. He also enlarged the Great Mosque, adding a domed and vaulted hall that remains one of the finest examples of early Swahili architecture.

## Ibn Battuta's visit

Around 1331 the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta arrived in Kilwa. He had already travelled across North Africa, Arabia and the Middle East. He wrote that Kilwa was one of the most beautiful and best-built towns in the world, built entirely of timber, though historians note that its great buildings were of coral stone.

Ibn Battuta described the sultan's piety and generosity: he raided the lands of non-Muslims on the mainland and gave much of the booty to the poor and to scholars. He also recorded the sultan humbly giving his own clothes to a beggar.

His account is one of the most important outside descriptions of the Swahili coast at its height.

## Daily life

Kilwa's wealthy merchants lived in stone houses with courtyards, carved plaster decorations, and wall niches displaying imported Chinese porcelain. Most townspeople lived in houses of wood, mud and thatch. Fishing, farming on the mainland and crafts such as weaving and bead-making supported the city.

Islam shaped public life. Scholars, judges and religious teachers were respected, and the city was part of a wider Muslim world stretching from Morocco to Indonesia.

## Decline

In the late fourteenth century the city faced plague, internal disputes and changes in the gold trade. Then, in 1505, a Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida attacked Kilwa, looted it and built a fort, known today as the Gereza. The Portuguese tried to control the gold trade themselves, but they disrupted it, and Kilwa's wealth faded.

In later centuries Kilwa revived somewhat under Omani influence, but now its trade was in enslaved people sent to the French islands of the Indian Ocean and to Zanzibar. The centre of activity moved to Kilwa Kivinje on the mainland.

## Kilwa today

In 1981 the ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and nearby Songo Mnara were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Visitors can walk through the Great Mosque, the palace of Husuni Kubwa, the Gereza fort and the remains of houses and tombs. For some years the site was on the list of World Heritage in Danger because of erosion and decay; conservation work, much of it by Tanzanian experts and local communities, removed it from that list in 2014.

## Why it matters

Kilwa proves that East Africa had wealthy, literate, cosmopolitan cities long before European colonialism. Its story is a story of Africa at the centre of a global trading world, connected to Asia and the Middle East for a thousand years.

## The Kilwa Chronicle

Much of what we know of Kilwa's rulers comes from the Kilwa Chronicle, which survives in two forms: an Arabic text known as the Kitab al-Sulwa, and a version recorded by the sixteenth-century Portuguese historian João de Barros. The chronicle lists sultans, wars, and successions, and tells the founding legend of the Shirazi prince.

Historians use the chronicle carefully. Its dates do not always match the evidence of coins and archaeology, and it was written to support the claims of particular rulers. But combined with excavation, it allows a remarkably detailed history of a medieval African city.

## Songo Mnara

A few kilometres south of Kilwa Kisiwani lies the island town of Songo Mnara, built mainly in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Its ruins include dozens of stone houses, several mosques, and an open space at the centre that may have been used for gatherings. Excavations there have revealed how ordinary daily life worked: cooking, weaving, bead-making, and children's games, as well as wealthy households with imported goods.

## How Swahili builders worked

Swahili builders used coral rag, rough blocks of fossil coral cut from the reef or the land, set in lime mortar made by burning coral. Floors and roofs were supported by mangrove poles, which grow straight and resist insects, and which became an important export to Arabia. Walls were plastered and often decorated with carved niches. Domes and vaults, like those of Kilwa's Great Mosque, show great skill.

These methods, adapted over centuries, are still visible in the stone towns of Zanzibar, Lamu and Bagamoyo.

## Archaeology in our time

The British archaeologist Neville Chittick excavated at Kilwa from 1958 to 1965 and established much of its history. More recent work by archaeologists including Stephanie Wynne-Jones and Jeffrey Fleisher, working with Tanzanian researchers and communities, has focused on how people lived, not only on kings and mosques. Local residents of Kilwa have been trained as site guides and conservation workers, linking today's community to its remarkable past.

## Kilwa among the Swahili towns

Kilwa was one of dozens of Swahili towns along roughly 3,000 kilometres of coast, from Mogadishu in the north to Sofala in the south. Each town was independent, ruled by its own sultan or council, and they competed fiercely for trade. Mombasa and Malindi were rivals; Pate and Lamu struggled for power in the north; Kilwa dominated the south.

What united them was a shared culture: the Kiswahili language, Islam, stone architecture, Indian Ocean trade, and family networks that crossed from town to town and across the sea.

## Kilwa in Swahili memory

In Swahili tradition Kilwa is remembered as a city of wealth and learning, and its founding legend is told on the coast to this day. The name Kilwa still lives in Kilwa Masoko, the district's modern town, and Kilwa Kivinje, a historic town on the mainland with old buildings from the Omani and German periods.

For many Tanzanians, the ruins are a source of pride, showing that their coast was part of a great civilisation centuries before colonial rule.

## Timeline

800s: People are living and trading on Kilwa island.
1000s–1100s: The Kilwa Chronicle's legendary Shirazi founding; early mosque building.
Late 1200s: The Mahdali dynasty comes to power; Kilwa controls the Sofala gold trade.
Early 1300s: Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman builds Husuni Kubwa and enlarges the Great Mosque.
c. 1331: Ibn Battuta visits Kilwa.
Late 1300s–1400s: Decline from plague, disputes and changes in trade.
1505: Portuguese forces under Francisco de Almeida sack Kilwa and build a fort.
1700s: Revival under Omani influence, with trade in enslaved people.
1958–1965: Excavations by Neville Chittick.
1981: Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

## Sources

Neville Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974). Ibn Battuta, The Travels (Rihla). Mark Horton and John Middleton, The Swahili (2000). Stephanie Wynne-Jones, A Material Culture (2016).

sw.title: Ibn Battuta azuru Kilwa
sw.text: Msafiri kutoka Morocco, Ibn Battuta, aliizuru Kilwa, mji tajiri wa biashara wa Waswahili kwenye pwani ya Afrika Mashariki, na akauelezea kuwa mmoja wa miji mizuri zaidi duniani.

en.title: Gutenberg's printing press
en.text:
Around 1440, a goldsmith from Mainz named Johannes Gutenberg began developing a new way to make books. His invention, a printing press using movable metal type, would change how knowledge spread across Europe and the world.

Before then, books in Europe were mostly copied by hand, often by monks, which took months or years for a single book. Woodblock printing existed, but carving a whole page into wood was slow.

Gutenberg's system combined several ideas. He cast individual letters in metal using a hand mould, so thousands of identical letters could be made and rearranged. He used an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and adapted a screw press, like those used for wine and olives, to press paper evenly onto the inked type.

His most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455. About 180 copies were made, and 49 survive today, some of the most valuable books in the world.

Printing was not new everywhere. In China, Bi Sheng made movable type from clay around 1040, and in Korea the Jikji, a Buddhist text printed with metal type in 1377, is the oldest surviving book made this way. But Gutenberg's press fitted the alphabets of Europe well and spread fast.

By 1500, printing presses were working in more than 250 European cities and millions of books had been printed. Cheap books fed the Renaissance, the Protestant Reformation and the Scientific Revolution, and helped ideas travel faster than any ruler could stop them.

sw.title: Mashine ya uchapishaji ya Gutenberg
sw.text: Johannes Gutenberg alibuni mashine ya uchapishaji yenye herufi za chuma zinazohamishika. Vitabu vikaweza kutengenezwa haraka na kwa bei nafuu, na maarifa yakaenea kwa kasi kuliko wakati wowote.

en.title: Vasco da Gama reaches the East African coast
en.text:
In July 1497 the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with four ships, hoping to reach India by sea. In early 1498, after rounding the Cape of Good Hope, his fleet arrived on the East African coast.

What the Portuguese found surprised them. The Swahili coast was a world of wealthy trading towns: Mozambique Island, Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Lamu and others. Stone mosques and houses lined the shore, and ships from Arabia, Persia, India and China called there. The Portuguese had come from a poorer corner of Europe into one of the richest trading systems on Earth.

At Mozambique Island and then at Mombasa, tensions quickly grew. In Mombasa, the Portuguese were received with suspicion, and fighting nearly broke out. They sailed on to Malindi, Mombasa's rival, where the sultan welcomed them and provided an experienced pilot who knew the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean.

With his help, da Gama crossed to Calicut in India, arriving on 20 May 1498. The sea route from Europe to Asia was open.

For East Africa, the arrival was the start of a violent century. Portuguese fleets attacked Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505, demanding tribute and trying to control trade. In 1593 they built Fort Jesus in Mombasa, which still stands.

Swahili towns resisted, and in 1698 forces from Oman captured Fort Jesus, ending Portuguese power north of Mozambique. But the arrival of 1498 had begun the long age of European empires in the Indian Ocean.

sw.title: Vasco da Gama afika pwani ya Afrika Mashariki
sw.text: Mvumbuzi wa Kireno Vasco da Gama alizunguka Rasi ya Tumaini Jema na kufika Mombasa na Malindi akiwa njiani kwenda India — mwanzo wa ushawishi wa Wareno kwenye pwani ya Waswahili.

en.title: The East African slave trade and the closing of Zanzibar's market
en.place: Zanzibar and the caravan routes of East Africa
en.text:
## A market in Stone Town

In the heart of Stone Town, Zanzibar, stands Christ Church Cathedral. Below it, in dark underground chambers, enslaved people were once held before being sold. On 5 June 1873, the slave market that stood on this spot was closed by treaty. But the story behind it stretches across half a continent.

## An old trade that grew

Slavery and the trade in people existed in East Africa and the Indian Ocean for many centuries, as in many parts of the world. Enslaved Africans were taken to Arabia, Persia and India, sometimes in small numbers.

In the nineteenth century the trade grew enormously. The main reason was the rise of Zanzibar as a plantation economy and trading centre under the rulers of Oman.

## The Omani sultans and the clove

The Busaidi sultans of Oman had long controlled parts of the Swahili coast. Sultan Seyyid Said saw the economic promise of Zanzibar, and from the 1830s he spent more and more time there, finally making it his main capital around 1840.

Cloves had been introduced to Zanzibar in the early nineteenth century. The islands of Unguja and Pemba proved perfect for growing them, and Zanzibar soon became the world's largest producer. Clove plantations needed huge numbers of workers, and those workers were enslaved Africans brought from the mainland.

Zanzibar also became the main market of the region. Enslaved people were sent from there to plantations on Pemba, to the coastal sugar and grain estates of Kenya, to Arabia and Persia, and, in earlier decades, to French plantations on the islands of Réunion and Mauritius.

## The caravan routes

To meet the demand, caravans of traders went deep into the interior. The central route left the coast at Bagamoyo and passed through Tabora, a major trading centre, to Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika, and beyond into the Congo. A southern route ran from Kilwa toward Lake Nyasa.

The caravans traded cloth, beads, guns and other goods for ivory and captives. Some captives were taken in raids and wars, which the trade itself encouraged. Some African rulers and traders took part, selling captives from rival groups. Coastal Swahili and Arab merchants financed and led many caravans. The most famous trader, Hamad bin Muhammad al-Murjabi, known as Tippu Tip, built a commercial empire in the eastern Congo.

Captives were forced to walk hundreds of kilometres to the coast, often chained together and made to carry ivory. Many died on the way from hunger, disease and violence. Those too weak to continue were sometimes abandoned or killed.

A popular tradition says the name Bagamoyo comes from "bwaga moyo", "lay down your heart", the despair of captives who reached the coast knowing they would never return. Historians debate the true origin of the name, but the meaning has become part of the town's memory.

## The scale of suffering

Exact numbers are impossible to know. Historians estimate that in the mid-nineteenth century, tens of thousands of people a year passed through Zanzibar's market at the trade's peak. Many more died on the routes before reaching the coast. In total, the East African trades of the nineteenth century took the lives and freedom of hundreds of thousands, probably more than a million people.

## Britain's pressure

Britain had abolished the slave trade in its empire in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833. It then used treaties and its navy to suppress the trade elsewhere. The Moresby Treaty of 1822 and the Hamerton Treaty of 1845 restricted the trade from Zanzibar's ports, but it continued on a large scale.

The writings of the missionary and explorer David Livingstone, who described massacres and the suffering of captives in the interior, shocked British public opinion. In 1873 Britain sent Sir Bartle Frere to Zanzibar, and the British consul John Kirk pressed Sultan Barghash bin Said, backed by the threat of a naval blockade. On 5 June 1873 Barghash signed a treaty banning the seaborne slave trade and closing the public market.

## Not the end

The treaty did not free anyone who was already enslaved. Smuggling continued, and caravans moved captives by land up the coast. Further decrees in 1876 restricted the land trade. The legal status of slavery itself was abolished in Zanzibar only in 1897, and on the mainland under German rule slavery was phased out slowly. Many freed people had nowhere to go, and some lived in settlements created by missions, such as at Bagamoyo and Mbweni.

## The cathedral and the memorial

On the site of the market, the Anglican Universities' Mission to Central Africa built Christ Church Cathedral between 1873 and 1879, under Bishop Edward Steere. Tradition holds that the altar stands on the spot of the old whipping post.

Next to it, a moving sculpture by the Swedish artist Clara Sörnäs, unveiled in 1998, shows five enslaved figures standing in a pit, with real chains around their necks. The underground chambers can be visited, and the site's museum tells the story of the trade and its victims.

## Different views

This history is sensitive and sometimes contested. Some accounts written in the colonial era emphasised the role of Arab traders and presented European colonisation as a humanitarian rescue, ignoring Europe's own enormous Atlantic slave trade and the forced labour of colonial rule. Some accounts minimise the role of African rulers and traders. Historians today try to tell the whole story honestly: a trade driven by global demand, involving many participants, that destroyed countless African lives.

## Why it matters

The legacy of the trade is still visible in East Africa: in the populations of the islands and coast, in the spread of Kiswahili into the interior along the caravan routes, and in communities of African descent in Arabia, Iran and India. Remembering it honours those who suffered and reminds us of the cost of treating human beings as property.

## Life on the plantations

On the clove plantations of Unguja and Pemba, enslaved people cleared land, planted and tended trees, and picked the clove buds by hand during the harvest season, which was the hardest time of the year. Outside the harvest, many were allowed to grow food on small plots, and some worked for wages or traded in town. Conditions varied greatly by owner: some enslaved people built families and communities, while others suffered extreme cruelty.

In the towns, enslaved people worked as porters, servants, craftsmen and sailors. Some rose to positions of trust, and freed people could become traders themselves.

## Resistance and escape

Enslaved people resisted in many ways: working slowly, running away, and forming communities of escaped people. On the Kenyan coast, groups of runaways known as watoro built settlements in the bush, and some defended themselves against attempts to recapture them. Others fled to mission stations, which sometimes offered refuge and sometimes returned people to their owners.

## Livingstone's last journey

David Livingstone, whose reports from the interior helped turn British opinion against the trade, died in 1873 in Chitambo, in today's Zambia. His African companions, led by Chuma and Susi, embalmed his body, wrapped it, and carried it for months, more than a thousand kilometres, to the coast at Bagamoyo in 1874, so that it could be returned to Britain.

That journey is one of the most remarkable acts of loyalty in East African history. The arrival of his body at Bagamoyo is commemorated at the town's old mission, and Chuma and Susi later travelled to Britain to help with his burial at Westminster Abbey.

## Bagamoyo today

Bagamoyo, once the terminus of the central caravan route, is now a quiet historic town and a candidate for UNESCO World Heritage status. Its old caravan serai, German boma, Catholic mission museum and ruins of the medieval town of Kaole tell layers of its history. It is also a centre of the arts, home to the Taasisi ya Sanaa na Utamaduni Bagamoyo (TaSUBa), Tanzania's leading arts and culture college.

## A language carried inland

One lasting effect of the caravan trade was the spread of Kiswahili. Coastal traders, porters and settlers carried the language along the routes to Tabora, Ujiji and beyond, where it became the language of trade. By the time Germany arrived, Kiswahili was widely understood across the interior, which is one reason it later became the language of colonial administration and then of Tanzanian nationalism.

The same routes also carried Islam, new foods, cloth and building styles into the interior. Towns like Tabora and Ujiji grew into mixed communities of coastal and inland people, and they remain important centres today.

## Timeline

1822: The Moresby Treaty restricts the slave trade from Zanzibar's ports.
c. 1840: Sultan Seyyid Said makes Zanzibar his main capital.
1845: The Hamerton Treaty further limits the trade.
1873: The slave market is closed on 5 June.
1874: Livingstone's body is carried to Bagamoyo by Chuma, Susi and their companions.
1876: Decrees restrict the overland trade.
1897: The legal status of slavery is abolished in Zanzibar.
1998: The memorial sculpture is unveiled beside Christ Church Cathedral.

## Sources

Abdul Sheriff, Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar (1987). Frederick Cooper, Plantation Slavery on the East Coast of Africa (1977). Edward Alpers, Ivory and Slaves in East Central Africa (1975).

sw.text: Kwa mkataba na Uingereza, Sultani Barghash alilifunga soko la watumwa la Zanzibar. Baadaye kanisa kuu lilijengwa mahali lilipokuwa soko hilo.

en.title: The Berlin Conference begins
en.text:
On 15 November 1884, representatives of 14 countries met in Berlin, invited by the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck. They came to agree on rules for European expansion in Africa. Not a single African was invited.

By the 1880s, European powers were racing to claim African land, a period later called the Scramble for Africa. Britain, France, Portugal, Germany and King Leopold II of Belgium all had ambitions, and they feared that rivalry over Africa could lead to war in Europe.

The conference lasted until 26 February 1885. Its General Act declared free trade in the Congo basin and on the Niger River, and recognised Leopold's claim to a vast area that became the Congo Free State, ruled as his personal property. Under Leopold, millions of Congolese suffered forced labour, mutilation and death in the rubber trade.

The conference also set the principle of "effective occupation": a European power claiming African territory had to notify the others and show that it controlled the area. This encouraged a rush of treaties, often signed under pressure or misunderstanding, and military expeditions.

The Berlin Conference did not draw every border in Africa, but it set the rules for the partition that followed. By 1914, almost the whole continent was under European rule. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

Many of today's African borders were drawn in European capitals, cutting across peoples, kingdoms and trade routes. When the OAU was founded in 1963, African states chose to keep these borders to avoid conflict, but their legacy still shapes the continent.

sw.title: Mkutano wa Berlin waanza
sw.text: Mataifa ya Ulaya yalikutana Berlin kuweka kanuni za kugawana ardhi ya Afrika. Hakuna kiongozi wa Kiafrika aliyealikwa. Mkutano huo uliharakisha 'Kinyang'anyiro cha Afrika' cha kikoloni.

en.title: Victory at Adwa
en.text:
On 1 March 1896, in the mountains near the town of Adwa in northern Ethiopia, the army of Emperor Menelik II defeated an invading Italian army. It was the greatest victory of an African nation over a European colonial army in the age of empire.

The conflict began with a treaty. In 1889 Menelik and Italy signed the Treaty of Wuchale. The Amharic text of Article 17 said Ethiopia could use Italy to conduct its foreign affairs. The Italian text said it must. Italy claimed Ethiopia was now its protectorate. Menelik rejected the claim and later renounced the treaty.

Italy, which already held Eritrea, invaded. Menelik called on Ethiopians from every region to defend the country. Empress Taytu Betul, his wife, was a key strategist and commanded troops herself. Ethiopia had also bought modern rifles and artillery.

At Adwa, Italian general Oreste Baratieri divided his forces of about 17,000 to 18,000 men into columns that lost contact with each other in the rough terrain. The Ethiopian army, probably around 100,000 strong, attacked each column separately. By midday the Italians were routed, with around 6,000 killed and thousands captured.

In October 1896 the Treaty of Addis Ababa recognised Ethiopia's full independence. Ethiopia remained free while almost all of Africa was colonised.

Adwa became a symbol of African resistance and dignity. The green, yellow and red of Ethiopia's flag inspired the flags of many African nations after independence. The victory is celebrated in Ethiopia every year on 2 March, Adwa Victory Day, by the Ethiopian calendar.

sw.title: Ushindi wa Adwa
sw.text: Majeshi ya Ethiopia yakiongozwa na Mfalme Menelik II yalishinda jeshi la Italia huko Adwa. Ushindi huo ulilinda uhuru wa Ethiopia na ukawa alama ya upinzani wa Afrika dhidi ya ukoloni.

en.title: The Maji Maji Uprising (1905–1907)
en.text:
## The land before the war

At the start of the twentieth century, the south of what is now Tanzania was home to many different peoples: the Matumbi and Ngindo in the hills behind Kilwa, the Pogoro and Mbunga around Mahenge, the Zaramo near the coast, and the powerful Ngoni in the far south around Songea. They were farmers, hunters and traders. Some had their own chiefs, others lived in small independent villages. They did not share one language or one ruler.

What they shared, by 1905, was a new master. In the 1880s the German adventurer Carl Peters had signed treaties with local leaders, often through trickery, and in 1891 the German government took direct control of a territory it called German East Africa.

The conquest was violent and was resisted from the start. On the coast, Abushiri bin Salim led an uprising in 1888–89 and was hanged at Pangani. In the southern highlands, the Hehe under Chief Mkwawa destroyed a German column at Lugalo in 1891 and fought on for years. Mkwawa took his own life in 1898 rather than be captured. German rule rested on these defeats, on military posts called bomas, and on fear.

## Cotton, taxes and the whip

In the early 1900s, Germany wanted its colony to pay for itself. Governor Gustav Adolf von Götzen, appointed in 1901, pushed a scheme to grow cotton for the textile factories of Germany.

From 1902, in the districts around Dar es Salaam and Kilwa, villages were ordered to work on communal cotton plots. Men and women had to leave their own fields for days at a time, often in the most important weeks of the farming season. The pay was tiny, and sometimes nothing at all after officials took their share. In many areas the soil was poor for cotton, so the harvests were small and the work felt pointless.

The scheme was enforced by akidas, government agents who were often outsiders to the communities they ruled, and by jumbes, village headmen. They used the kiboko, a hippo-hide whip, on people who refused or worked too slowly. A new hut tax also had to be paid in cash, forcing people to sell crops or work for others.

Anger built across the south. People complained of hunger, humiliation and the loss of their own food. But each village alone was weak against German rifles and machine guns. What they needed was something to unite them.

## Kinjikitile and the sacred water

That unity came from a spiritual leader. In the village of Ngarambe lived a man named Kinjikitile Ngwale. In 1904 he was said to have been taken by a spirit called Hongo, linked to the powerful shrine of Bokero near the Rufiji River.

Kinjikitile taught that the ancestors were unhappy and that the Germans would be driven out. He gave his followers maji, water mixed with castor oil and millet seeds, as protective medicine. Those who received it, he said, would be protected; German bullets would turn to water.

People came to Ngarambe from far away, and messengers carried the medicine to other areas. Drinking the same water created a bond between peoples who had never been allies, and in some cases had been enemies. Historians see it as one of the first movements in East Africa that brought many different groups together against colonial rule.

## The outbreak: July 1905

In late July 1905, in the Matumbi Hills at a place called Nandete, villagers went to a German cotton field and uprooted the plants. It was a deliberate act of defiance, and it started the war.

The fighters attacked a trading post at Samanga on the coast and the German post at Kibata. Akidas, missionaries and settlers were killed, and mission stations burned. Within weeks the uprising had spread through Ngindo country towards Liwale, where the German post was destroyed.

The Germans arrested Kinjikitile and hanged him in August 1905. But the movement no longer depended on one man. The water had already travelled.

## The war spreads

The uprising moved west and south like fire through dry grass. Pogoro, Mbunga, Bena and many other communities joined. In all, more than twenty peoples took part, across much of the southern half of the colony.

The greatest test of the water came at Mahenge on 30 August 1905. Thousands of fighters, believing they were protected, advanced in waves toward the German fort. Behind its walls, German officers and African askari soldiers waited with machine guns. Wave after wave was cut down, and hundreds died in front of the walls.

The defeat at Mahenge shook faith in the water. Some said the dead had broken the rules of the medicine. The war continued, but many began to doubt.

In September the Ngoni of Songea joined, under leaders including Chabruma and Songea Mbano. They were experienced soldiers, and their entry made the war more dangerous for the Germans in the far south.

## Fire and famine

Germany rushed in reinforcements: marines from warships, more askari from other parts of the colony, and troops from as far as New Guinea. Their firepower was overwhelming, but the fighters avoided open battle and kept up a guerrilla war from forests and hills.

So the German commanders chose a policy that targeted everyone. Columns marched through the south burning villages, crops and food stores, and seizing livestock. The aim was to starve the resistance into surrender, and it worked.

The result was a terrible famine in 1906 and 1907. Whole regions emptied. Women, children and the elderly, who had never carried a spear, died in their tens of thousands. Many survivors fled into the bush or to other districts.

In February 1906 at Songea, the Germans hanged dozens of resistance leaders, including Songea Mbano. Their mass grave is now part of the Maji Maji Memorial Museum. The last pockets of resistance were crushed in 1907.

## The cost

No one knows exactly how many people died. German officials at the time admitted around 75,000 deaths. Later historians, using population records and evidence of famine, estimate between about 100,000 and 300,000, most of them from hunger. A small number of Europeans and several hundred askari were also killed.

Parts of southern Tanzania took decades to recover. Some farmed areas turned into wild bush, and later game reserves such as the Selous, today Nyerere National Park, grew over once-inhabited land.

## Different ways of seeing it

German officials at the time described the uprising as a superstitious revolt stirred up by witchcraft. The war came at the same time as Germany's genocide of the Herero and Nama in German South West Africa, today's Namibia.

African memory, passed down in families and collected by Tanzanian historians in the 1960s in the Maji Maji Research Project led by G. C. K. Gwassa, shows the war as a struggle for land, food, dignity and freedom. Elders spoke of hunger, the whip and the cotton plots, not only of the water.

Historians still debate how far the uprising was one movement or many local wars joined by a shared idea. The British historian John Iliffe argued that Maji Maji was an early attempt to build unity across ethnic lines, using religion as the bridge. Others stress each community's local reasons for fighting. Both views agree that forced cotton growing lit the fire.

## What came after

The disaster forced changes. Under Governor Albrecht von Rechenberg, from 1906, forced communal cotton growing was stopped, the worst abuses of akidas were restricted, and Africans were encouraged to grow cash crops on their own farms. German rule continued until Germany lost the colony in the First World War.

## Why it matters today

For Tanzanian nationalists, Maji Maji became a symbol of the first great unity of the country's peoples against foreign rule. Julius Nyerere often spoke of it as a lesson: the people were defeated because they fought with faith in magic and without organisation, but their courage showed what unity could do. TANU's peaceful, organised struggle in the 1950s was in a sense built on that lesson.

The war lives on in Tanzanian culture. Ebrahim Hussein's Swahili play "Kinjeketile" (1969) is studied in schools, and the football club Majimaji FC of Songea carries the name.

In 2023 the President of Germany, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, visited the museum in Songea. He said he was ashamed of what German colonial soldiers had done and asked for forgiveness. Descendants of the victims asked for more: the return of ancestral remains taken to Germany and full recognition of the harm done.

## Africans on both sides

The German colonial army, the Schutztruppe, was made up mostly of African soldiers called askari. Many had been recruited from Sudan, Somalia and other parts of German East Africa, and some came from peoples who had their own reasons to fight the rebels. Thousands of African porters carried the army's loads. Some communities that had suffered raids from neighbours chose to side with the Germans, and auxiliaries from these groups joined the campaigns.

This meant that Maji Maji was not simply Africans against Europeans. It was a colonial war in which Africans died on both sides, and in which the heaviest suffering fell on ordinary villagers caught between armies.

## Women and the home front

Women's experiences are less recorded but were central. Women worked the cotton plots, grew the food that fed the fighters, carried messages and medicine, and bore the worst of the famine that followed. Oral histories collected later describe women hiding children and grain in the forests and walking long distances in search of food. Their survival rebuilt the communities after the war.

## Sources

John Iliffe, A Modern History of Tanganyika (1979). G. C. K. Gwassa and John Iliffe (eds.), Records of the Maji Maji Rising (1967). Jamie Monson, "Relocating Maji Maji", Journal of African History (1998). Ebrahim Hussein, Kinjeketile (1969).

sw.title: Vita vya Maji Maji vyaanza
sw.text: Jamii za kusini mwa Tanganyika ziliinuka dhidi ya utawala wa kikoloni wa Wajerumani na kilimo cha lazima cha pamba. Vita hivyo vilizimwa kufikia 1907, lakini vinakumbukwa kama moja ya mapambano makubwa dhidi ya ukoloni barani Afrika.

en.title: The Berlin Wall falls
en.text:
On the evening of 9 November 1989, crowds of East Germans gathered at the border crossings in Berlin. By midnight, guards had opened the gates. People streamed through, crying, laughing and climbing onto the Berlin Wall. The wall that had divided the city for 28 years had fallen.

After the Second World War, Germany was divided into a democratic West and a communist East. Berlin, deep inside East Germany, was also split. Millions of East Germans fled west through Berlin. To stop them, on 13 August 1961 the East German government began building a wall, which grew into a heavily guarded barrier more than 150 kilometres long around West Berlin.

Families were separated overnight. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross the wall in Berlin.

By 1989 the communist world was changing. Mikhail Gorbachev in the Soviet Union allowed more openness, Hungary opened its border with Austria, and huge peaceful protests filled the streets of East German cities.

On 9 November a government spokesman, Günter Schabowski, announced new travel rules at a press conference. Asked when they would start, he looked at his notes and said they applied immediately. The news spread on television. Crowds gathered at Bornholmer Straße, and at about 11:30 p.m. the officer in charge, unable to hold them back, opened the gate.

Within weeks, people were chipping pieces off the wall. Less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was reunited. The fall of the Berlin Wall became the symbol of the end of the Cold War.

sw.title: Ukuta wa Berlin waanguka
sw.text: Mamlaka ya Ujerumani Mashariki yalifungua vivuko vya mpaka katika Ukuta wa Berlin, na umati ukaanza kuubomoa. Ujerumani iliunganishwa tena chini ya mwaka mmoja baadaye.

en.title: The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent
en.text:
Around 11,500 years ago, in a band of land curving from the Nile valley through the Levant and southern Turkey down to the rivers of Iraq, people began to do something new. Instead of only gathering wild plants and hunting animals, they started planting seeds and keeping animals close. This change, often called the Neolithic Revolution, transformed human life more than almost anything before it.

The region is known as the Fertile Crescent. Wild wheat, barley, lentils and peas grew there naturally, along with wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. Over many generations, people chose the best seeds and the calmest animals, slowly creating domesticated crops and livestock.

At Göbekli Tepe in southern Turkey, people built huge carved stone pillars around 9500 BCE, before farming was fully established. Some archaeologists think gathering for great feasts at such places may have encouraged people to grow more food.

Farming allowed people to settle in villages such as Jericho and Çatalhöyük, store food, and support larger populations. It also brought new problems: hard labour, diseases spreading from animals, and arguments over land and stored wealth.

Farming was not invented in only one place. Over the following thousands of years it began independently in China (rice and millet), New Guinea, Mesoamerica (maize, beans and squash), the Andes (potatoes), and in Africa, where sorghum, pearl millet, yams and African rice were domesticated, and cattle herding spread across the Sahara when it was green.

Almost every city, kingdom and invention that came later was built on the food surplus that farming made possible.

en.title: Writing is invented in Sumer
en.text:
Around 3200 BCE, in the city of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, scribes pressed marks into wet clay with reed pens. They were keeping records of grain, beer, sheep and workers. Out of these simple accounts grew one of humanity's greatest inventions: writing.

Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in today's Iraq, was home to the Sumerians, who built some of the first cities. Uruk may have had more than 40,000 people. Running temples and storehouses for so many needed a way to remember who owed what.

The earliest signs were pictures: a jar, a head of grain, an ox. Over centuries they became wedge-shaped marks, which we call cuneiform, from the Latin word for wedge. Signs came to stand for sounds as well as things, so scribes could write names, laws, letters, prayers and stories.

Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years and adapted for many languages, including Akkadian, Babylonian, Assyrian and Hittite. Hundreds of thousands of clay tablets survive, because clay hardens when baked, and libraries burned in wars actually preserved their tablets.

Writing was invented separately in other places too: Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at almost the same time, Chinese writing by about 1200 BCE, and the Maya and other peoples of Mesoamerica developed their own scripts.

Writing allowed laws to be fixed, history to be recorded, and stories like the Epic of Gilgamesh to survive thousands of years. It marks the boundary between what historians call prehistory and history.

en.title: The Code of Hammurabi
en.text:
Around 1754 BCE, King Hammurabi of Babylon set up a tall black stone pillar carved with nearly 300 laws. At the top, a carving shows the king standing before Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. The Code of Hammurabi is one of the oldest and most complete written law collections in the world.

Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. Through war and diplomacy he united much of Mesopotamia under Babylon. Publishing laws helped show that the king ruled justly and brought order to his many peoples.

The laws cover everyday life: trade and prices, loans and debt, farming and irrigation, marriage and divorce, inheritance, adoption, theft, building work and medical care. One law says that if a builder's house collapses and kills its owner, the builder shall be put to death.

Some punishments follow the rule of "an eye for an eye": if a man destroys another man's eye, his own eye shall be destroyed. But the laws were not equal for everyone. Punishments differed for nobles, ordinary free people and enslaved people.

Hammurabi was not the first lawgiver. Earlier codes, such as that of Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE, existed. But his stele is the best preserved. It was carried off as war booty to Susa in Iran in the twelfth century BCE, where French archaeologists found it in 1901. Today it stands in the Louvre Museum in Paris.

The idea that laws should be written down and known to all, rather than kept only in the mind of the ruler, is a foundation of legal systems today.

en.title: The Kushite kings rule Egypt
en.text:
Around 747 BCE, King Piye of Kush marched north from his capital at Napata, in today's Sudan, and conquered Egypt. For nearly a century, kings from Kush ruled both lands as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt, sometimes called the Black Pharaohs.

Kush lay along the Nile south of Egypt, in the region called Nubia. It was one of Africa's earliest great kingdoms, rich in gold, ivory, ebony and skilled archers. For centuries Egypt had controlled Nubia, but as Egypt split into rival states, Kush grew strong.

Piye recorded his campaign on a great stone stela. He presented himself as a devoted follower of the god Amun, restoring order to a divided Egypt. He was famous for loving horses and punishing a defeated ruler for letting his horses go hungry.

His successors, including Shabaqo and Taharqa, ruled from Memphis and Thebes. Taharqa built temples across Egypt and Nubia. The Kushite kings revived old Egyptian traditions, and also built pyramids for their own tombs, a custom that Egypt itself had long abandoned.

In the 660s BCE the Assyrians drove the Kushites out of Egypt. Kush continued for another thousand years, later with its capital at Meroë, where more than 200 pyramids stand today, more than in all of Egypt. Meroë was a centre of iron-working, and its people developed their own script, Meroitic, which scholars still cannot fully read.

Kush shows that ancient Africa had powerful kingdoms that shaped the history of the Nile and the whole ancient world.

en.title: The Buddha's teaching begins
en.text:
Around the fifth century BCE, a man named Siddhartha Gautama sat in meditation beneath a tree at Bodh Gaya in northern India. According to Buddhist tradition, there he reached enlightenment, a complete understanding of suffering and how to end it. He became known as the Buddha, "the awakened one".

Siddhartha was born into a ruling family in Lumbini, in today's Nepal. Tradition says he grew up in comfort, protected from hardship, until he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a wandering holy man. Troubled, he left his palace to search for the meaning of suffering.

He tried extreme fasting and self-punishment, but found that this did not bring wisdom. Instead he taught a Middle Way between luxury and harsh denial.

He gave his first sermon in a deer park at Sarnath, near Varanasi. He taught the Four Noble Truths: life includes suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path, including right understanding, right speech, right action and right mindfulness.

The Buddha taught for about 45 years, welcoming people of every social class, including women, into his community of monks and nuns. Scholars debate the exact dates of his life.

In the third century BCE, the Indian emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism and sent missionaries far and wide. Buddhism spread to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, China, Korea, Japan and Tibet. Today hundreds of millions of people follow it, and ideas such as mindfulness meditation have spread around the world.

en.title: Democracy begins in Athens
en.text:
In 508 BCE, a leader named Cleisthenes introduced reforms in the Greek city of Athens that gave power to the ordinary citizens. The system came to be called demokratia, from the Greek words demos, the people, and kratos, power.

Before this, Athens had been ruled by aristocrats and tyrants. Cleisthenes reorganised citizens into ten new tribes that mixed people from the city, the coast and the countryside, breaking the power of old noble families.

The heart of Athenian democracy was the Assembly, which met on a hill called the Pnyx. Any male citizen could attend, speak and vote on war, peace, laws and taxes. Thousands came. A Council of 500, chosen by lot, prepared business. Many officials were chosen by lottery, not elections, so that ordinary citizens shared in government.

Athens even had ostracism: once a year citizens could write a name on a broken piece of pottery, and the person with the most votes, if enough were cast, was sent away for ten years. It was a way to stop anyone becoming too powerful.

But Athenian democracy was limited. Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in Athens could not vote. Only a minority of adults were full citizens.

Democracy in Athens survived, with interruptions, for nearly two centuries, a period when the city also produced great drama, philosophy and architecture, including the Parthenon. Its ideas, that the people should rule and that leaders must answer to citizens, inspired later democratic movements around the world.

en.title: Qin Shi Huang unites China
en.text:
In 221 BCE, King Zheng of the state of Qin completed the conquest of his last rival and united China under one ruler. He gave himself a new title, Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.

For more than two centuries, China had been divided among warring states. Qin, in the west, built a strong army and a strict system of laws under the philosophy known as Legalism, which held that people must be controlled by clear rewards and harsh punishments.

The First Emperor worked to make his huge empire one. He standardised weights, measures and coins, the width of cart axles so wagons could use the same roads, and above all the written script, so that people speaking different languages could read the same documents. That shared writing system helped hold China together for the next two thousand years.

He built roads and canals, and joined and extended earlier walls in the north into a long defensive line, an early form of the Great Wall. Hundreds of thousands of labourers worked on these projects, and many died.

He was also feared. His government is said to have burned books it considered dangerous and punished scholars who criticised it.

When he died in 210 BCE, he was buried in a vast tomb near Xi'an guarded by the Terracotta Army: thousands of life-size clay soldiers, each with a different face, discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974.

The Qin dynasty collapsed soon after his death, but the Han dynasty that followed kept the unified empire he had created. The word China itself may come from Qin.

en.title: King Ezana of Aksum adopts Christianity
en.text:
In the fourth century CE, King Ezana of Aksum, in today's northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, became a Christian. His kingdom became one of the first states in the world to adopt Christianity, and the church he supported, now the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, has continued ever since.

Aksum was one of the great powers of the ancient world. A Persian writer of the third century listed it with Rome, Persia and China as one of the four great kingdoms. Its port of Adulis on the Red Sea traded ivory, gold, incense and other goods with Egypt, Arabia, India and the Roman world.

Aksum minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze, one of very few ancient African states to do so. Its kings built giant stone obelisks, or stelae, to mark royal tombs. The tallest still standing is about 24 metres high, carved to look like a multi-storey building.

According to tradition, a young Christian from Tyre named Frumentius was shipwrecked and brought to the Aksumite court, where he educated the young Ezana. Frumentius later became the first bishop of Aksum. Ezana's coins show the change: early ones carry the crescent and disc of older gods, later ones the cross.

Aksum also developed the Ge'ez script, which is still used for the Amharic and Tigrinya languages today.

Aksum declined from the seventh century as trade routes changed. But it laid the foundations for the Christian kingdoms of Ethiopia, with their unique churches, manuscripts and traditions, including the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela built centuries later.

en.title: The last Western Roman emperor is deposed
en.text:
On 4 September 476, a Germanic military commander named Odoacer removed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus from his throne in Ravenna, Italy. Odoacer did not take the title of emperor himself. Instead he sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. Historians often use this moment to mark the end of the Western Roman Empire.

At its height in the second century CE, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps 60 million people. Its roads, laws, cities, aqueducts and Latin language shaped Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.

Rome's decline was long and had many causes. Civil wars between generals, economic troubles, plague, and the cost of defending enormous borders weakened the state. In 395 the empire was divided permanently into eastern and western halves.

From the late fourth century, groups such as the Goths, Vandals and Franks moved into Roman lands, sometimes as allies and soldiers, sometimes as invaders. Rome itself was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455. The Vandals also took the rich province of North Africa, around Carthage.

By 476 the western emperor controlled little more than Italy. Odoacer's act was quiet, almost symbolic.

The Eastern Roman Empire, which historians call the Byzantine Empire, continued for nearly a thousand years more, until Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. And Roman influence never really ended: Latin grew into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and Roman law still underlies many legal systems.

en.title: The Hijra: the Prophet Muhammad moves to Medina
en.text:
In 622 CE, the Prophet Muhammad and his followers left Mecca and moved to the oasis town of Yathrib, about 450 kilometres to the north. The town became known as Medina, the City of the Prophet. This journey, the Hijra, or migration, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Quraysh tribe. Mecca was a trading town and the site of the Kaaba, a shrine visited by pilgrims. According to Islamic tradition, around 610 he began receiving revelations from God through the angel Jibril (Gabriel), which were later collected as the Quran.

He preached that there is one God, and called for justice, care for the poor, orphans and widows, and moral responsibility. His message won followers, but many powerful Meccans opposed it because it challenged their religion and their trade in pilgrims. Muslims faced pressure and persecution, and some early Muslims took refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia.

In Medina, Muhammad became both religious and political leader. He set out an agreement, often called the Constitution of Medina, for the town's communities, including Jewish tribes. The first mosque was built there.

After years of conflict, Mecca came under Muslim control in 630. Muhammad died in Medina in 632.

Within a century, Islam spread from Spain to Central Asia. It later travelled along trade routes to West Africa, the Swahili coast and Southeast Asia, shaping language, architecture, law and learning. Today about a quarter of the world's people are Muslim, and the Islamic year is still counted from the Hijra.

en.title: The oldest dated printed book
en.text:
A copy of a Buddhist scripture called the Diamond Sutra, printed in China, carries a note at its end giving a date that corresponds to 11 May 868 CE. It is the oldest surviving printed book with a clear date, nearly 600 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

The book is a scroll about five metres long, made of sheets of paper pasted together. It was printed with carved wooden blocks: each whole page was cut in reverse into a block of wood, inked, and pressed onto paper. The opening picture shows the Buddha preaching to his disciple Subhuti, a finely detailed woodcut.

The note at the end says that a man named Wang Jie had the book made for free distribution, on behalf of his two parents. Printing scriptures to share was believed to bring spiritual merit.

The scroll was found in 1900 in a sealed cave library at Dunhuang, an oasis town on the Silk Road. The library had been closed up around the year 1000 and held tens of thousands of manuscripts in many languages. In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein took the scroll to Britain; it is now in the British Library, a fact that remains controversial.

China also invented paper, around the second century CE or earlier, and later movable type. Papermaking spread along the Silk Road to the Islamic world, where Baghdad had paper mills by the late eighth century, and from there to Europe.

The Diamond Sutra reminds us that printing has a long, global history, and that East Asia led the way.

en.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
en.text:
In 1206, at a great assembly called a kurultai near the Onon River, the chiefs of the Mongol tribes proclaimed a leader named Temüjin as their ruler. He took the title Genghis Khan, often understood as "universal ruler". Within 70 years, his family would rule the largest connected land empire in history.

Temüjin was born around 1162. His father was poisoned when he was a boy, and his family was abandoned by their clan, surviving by hunting and gathering. Through courage, loyal friendships and alliances, he rose to unite the feuding tribes of the steppe.

He reorganised Mongol society into military units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, mixing tribes to break old loyalties, and promoted people for ability rather than birth. Mongol horsemen were superb archers, moving faster than any army of the time, with several horses per rider.

The Mongols conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia and Russia, and later reached Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Cities that resisted, such as Merv, Nishapur and Baghdad in 1258, were destroyed with enormous loss of life. Millions died in the conquests.

Yet the empire also connected the world. Under Mongol rule, often called the Pax Mongolica, the Silk Roads were safer for merchants and travellers, including Marco Polo. Ideas, technologies and religions moved between China, Persia and Europe. The Mongols allowed freedom of religion and created a fast relay postal system.

Genghis Khan died in 1227. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered all of China and founded the Yuan dynasty. In Mongolia, Genghis Khan is honoured as the father of the nation.

en.title: Magna Carta is sealed
en.text:
On 15 June 1215, in a meadow called Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John of England set his seal on a document demanded by his rebellious barons. It became known as Magna Carta, the Great Charter.

King John was deeply unpopular. He had lost English lands in France, raised heavy taxes to pay for wars, and punished nobles without fair trial. In 1215 a group of barons rebelled and captured London.

Magna Carta was a peace treaty. Most of its 63 clauses dealt with the barons' specific complaints about inheritance, taxes, forests and debts. But a few clauses had a much bigger future. One said that no free man could be imprisoned, stripped of his rights or property, or punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land. Another said that justice would not be sold, denied or delayed.

The charter failed at first. Within weeks the Pope annulled it at John's request and civil war broke out. But after John died in 1216, the charter was reissued several times in revised form, and in 1225 it became part of English law.

Over the centuries Magna Carta grew into a symbol of the idea that rulers are subject to the law. It influenced the English Bill of Rights in 1689, the United States Constitution and Bill of Rights, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

At the time it protected only a small group of powerful men. Its later fame came from people who used its words to demand rights for everyone.

en.title: Great Zimbabwe at its height
en.text:
Around 1300, on a granite hilltop and the valley below in today's southern Zimbabwe, stood the largest stone city in sub-Saharan Africa. Its great walls were built from thousands of granite blocks fitted together without any mortar. Its name, Great Zimbabwe, comes from the Shona words for "houses of stone".

Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona people between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. At its height it may have been home to around 10,000 to 18,000 people. The Hill Complex was probably the home of the king and a religious centre. Below it, the Great Enclosure has an outer wall about 11 metres high and 250 metres long, with a mysterious solid conical tower inside.

The city's wealth came from cattle and from trade. Gold mined on the Zimbabwe plateau was carried to the coast at Sofala and sold to Swahili merchants of Kilwa, who shipped it across the Indian Ocean. Archaeologists at Great Zimbabwe have found glass beads from India, pottery from Persia and porcelain from China.

Eight carved soapstone birds were found at the site, probably symbols of royal ancestors. One of them is now on Zimbabwe's flag and coat of arms.

When European colonists arrived in the nineteenth century, many refused to believe Africans had built Great Zimbabwe, inventing theories about foreign builders. Archaeology proved them wrong, and the colonial government tried to suppress the truth.

When Rhodesia won independence in 1980, the new nation took the name Zimbabwe in honour of this city. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

en.title: The Black Death reaches Europe
en.text:
In October 1347, trading ships from the Black Sea docked at Messina in Sicily. Sailors on board were sick and dying. They had brought the bubonic plague, and within four years the disease known as the Black Death killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population.

The plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas that live on rats and other rodents. It probably began in Central Asia and spread along the trade routes of the Mongol world. In 1346 it reached Caffa, a trading port in Crimea, from where Italian ships carried it into the Mediterranean.

Victims developed painful swellings called buboes in the groin, armpits and neck, along with fever. Many died within days. A form that spread through the lungs could kill even faster.

The plague struck the Middle East and North Africa too. Cairo, one of the world's largest cities, lost a huge part of its people.

No one at the time understood the cause. Some blamed bad air, the stars or God's anger. Groups called flagellants whipped themselves in public. Terribly, many Jewish communities were falsely blamed for poisoning wells and were massacred.

The Black Death changed society. With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher wages, weakening the old feudal system. Cities created health boards, and Venice began isolating ships for 40 days, quaranta giorni, which gave us the word quarantine.

Plague returned many times over the following centuries. Today it is treatable with antibiotics, but the Black Death remains one of the deadliest pandemics in human history.

en.title: Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet sets sail
en.place: Nanjing, China, to the Indian Ocean
en.text:
In 1405, the first of seven great voyages left China under the command of Admiral Zheng He. His fleet of treasure ships was the largest the world had ever seen, and over the next 28 years it sailed as far as Arabia and the coast of East Africa.

Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan into a Muslim family. Captured as a boy by Ming armies, he became a court official and a trusted ally of the Yongle Emperor, who sent him to show China's power and wealth to the lands of the Indian Ocean.

The first fleet is said to have had more than 300 ships and nearly 28,000 people. The largest ships were described as many times larger than the ships of Columbus. Historians debate their exact size, but they were certainly enormous.

The fleets visited Southeast Asia, India, Sri Lanka, Hormuz in Persia, Arabia and the Swahili coast, including Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi. They brought silk, porcelain and gifts, and returned with spices, precious stones, ambassadors, and exotic animals. Malindi's envoys sent a giraffe to China, where it was celebrated as a qilin, a mythical creature of good fortune.

These were not voyages of conquest like the later European expeditions, but they did use force when challenged.

After the Yongle Emperor died, the Ming court turned inward. The voyages ended after 1433, records were reportedly destroyed, and building large ocean-going ships was restricted. Fragments of Chinese porcelain are still found along the East African coast, and legends in Kenya tell of shipwrecked Chinese sailors who stayed.

en.title: Oba Ewuare the Great rebuilds Benin
en.text:
Around 1440, a ruler named Ewuare became Oba, or king, of Benin, in the forests of what is now southern Nigeria. Remembered as Ewuare the Great, he turned the kingdom into a powerful empire and rebuilt its capital, Benin City, into one of the most impressive cities in Africa.

Ewuare strengthened the power of the Oba, created new councils of chiefs, and expanded the kingdom through war. He rebuilt Benin City with broad, straight streets and enormous earthworks. The walls and moats of Benin, built over centuries, may have stretched thousands of kilometres in total, one of the largest earthworks ever created before modern machines.

The court supported guilds of craftsmen. Bronze-casters, ivory carvers and wood carvers worked only for the Oba. Using the lost-wax method, they made thousands of brass plaques, heads and figures, recording kings, warriors, ceremonies and visitors. Together these are known as the Benin Bronzes.

Portuguese visitors arrived in the 1480s and described a large, well-ordered city. Benin traded pepper, cloth and ivory with Europeans, and later was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade.

In 1897, a British force attacked Benin City, burned it and looted thousands of the bronzes and ivories, which were sold and scattered to museums around the world. The Oba was exiled.

The kingdom of Benin and its Oba still exist today within Nigeria. In recent years, museums in Germany, Britain and elsewhere have begun returning Benin Bronzes, a long-awaited step toward repairing that historic theft.

en.title: The Maya city of Tikal at its height
en.text:
Around 700 CE, the city of Tikal, deep in the rainforests of today's Guatemala, was one of the greatest cities of the Maya world. Stone temple-pyramids rose above the trees, some more than 60 metres high, and tens of thousands of people lived in and around the city.

The Maya civilisation spread across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. Its Classic period, roughly 250 to 900 CE, was a time of many competing city-states, each ruled by a divine king, called k'uhul ajaw.

The Maya were remarkable scholars. They developed the most complete writing system of the ancient Americas, combining signs for words and syllables, carved on monuments and painted in folding books made of bark paper. They used the concept of zero and a counting system based on twenty. Their astronomers tracked the movements of the Sun, Moon and Venus with great precision, and their Long Count calendar recorded dates over thousands of years.

Tikal had a long rivalry with the city of Calakmul. Inscriptions record wars, alliances and captured kings. In 695, Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil defeated Calakmul, and he was buried in the famous Temple I.

Recent laser surveys from the air, called LiDAR, have revealed that the Maya lowlands held far more people than once thought, with roads, farms and defences hidden under the forest.

In the ninth century many southern Maya cities were abandoned, probably because of drought, warfare and environmental stress. But the Maya did not disappear. Millions of Maya people live in the region today and speak around 30 Maya languages.

en.title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
en.text:
On 12 October 1492, after more than two months at sea, three Spanish ships commanded by the Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas. Its Taíno inhabitants called it Guanahani. Columbus named it San Salvador and claimed it for the Spanish crown.

Columbus believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. He greatly underestimated the size of the Earth and had no idea that two continents lay in the way. Funded by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain, he left with the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María. Until his death he insisted he had reached the edge of Asia, which is why the islands were called the West Indies and their people "Indians".

The Americas were not empty or unknown. Tens of millions of people lived there, in societies ranging from small villages to the vast empires of the Aztecs and Incas. Norse sailors had also reached Newfoundland around the year 1000.

What followed was one of the biggest turning points in world history, often called the Columbian Exchange. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava and cocoa travelled to Europe, Africa and Asia. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar cane went west.

But diseases brought by Europeans, such as smallpox and measles, killed a huge share of Indigenous peoples, who had no immunity. Conquest, enslavement and forced labour destroyed many societies. To replace Indigenous workers, Europeans began transporting enslaved Africans across the Atlantic in enormous numbers.

For this reason, 12 October is marked very differently today: as Columbus Day in some places, and as Indigenous Peoples' Day or a day of resistance in others.

en.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
en.text:
On 13 August 1521, after a siege of about three months, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan fell to Spanish conquistadors led by Hernán Cortés and their many Indigenous allies. The last Aztec ruler, Cuauhtémoc, was captured as he tried to escape by canoe.

Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world, home to perhaps 200,000 people. It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected to the shore by long causeways, with canals, floating gardens called chinampas, markets, and the great twin temple of the Templo Mayor at its centre. Spanish soldiers wrote that it was more magnificent than any city they had seen in Europe.

The Mexica, as the Aztecs called themselves, ruled an empire that demanded tribute from many conquered peoples. Many of those peoples hated Aztec rule. Cortés, who landed in 1519 with only a few hundred Spaniards, gained tens of thousands of allies, especially from the city-state of Tlaxcala.

The Spanish were at first welcomed into the city by the emperor Moctezuma II, who was then taken prisoner and died in 1520. The Spanish were driven out, but returned with allies and boats built for the lake.

A smallpox epidemic, brought by the Europeans, had already killed huge numbers in the city, including Moctezuma's successor Cuitláhuac. The siege cut off food and water, and much of the city was destroyed in the fighting.

Mexico City was built on its ruins. The Templo Mayor was rediscovered in 1978 by electricity workers, and the eagle on a cactus, the symbol of Tenochtitlan's founding, is on Mexico's flag today.

en.title: The transatlantic slave trade
en.place: West and Central Africa to the Americas
en.text:
Around 1526, the first known ship carried enslaved Africans directly from Africa to the Americas. Over the next three and a half centuries, about 12.5 million African women, men and children were forced onto ships bound across the Atlantic. Around 10.7 million survived the voyage.

Europeans, especially the Portuguese, British, French, Spanish and Dutch, built forts and trading posts along the coast of West and Central Africa, such as Elmina in Ghana and Gorée in Senegal. They traded cloth, guns, alcohol and metal goods to African rulers and merchants in exchange for captives, many taken in wars and raids that the trade itself encouraged.

The journey across the ocean was called the Middle Passage. People were chained below deck in crowded, dark and filthy holds for weeks or months. Disease, violence and despair killed many. Some resisted, through revolts on board or by refusing to eat.

In the Americas, enslaved people were forced to work on plantations of sugar, tobacco, cotton and coffee, in mines and in houses. Brazil received the largest number, followed by the Caribbean. Their labour produced enormous wealth for Europe and the Americas.

Enslaved Africans resisted constantly: through escape, rebellion, preserving languages, music, religion and family. Their cultures shaped the Americas, from samba and jazz to food and faith.

The trade was abolished step by step in the nineteenth century, after campaigns by abolitionists and above all the resistance of enslaved people, including the Haitian Revolution. Its effects, including racism and inequality, are still felt on both sides of the Atlantic.

en.title: Queen Nzinga comes to power
en.text:
In 1624 Nzinga Mbande became ruler of Ndongo, a kingdom of the Mbundu people in what is now Angola. For nearly four decades she resisted Portuguese colonial expansion and the slave trade that came with it, becoming one of the most famous leaders in African history.

Portugal had established a colony at Luanda in 1575 and pushed inland, raiding for captives to ship to Brazil. Nzinga first appeared in history in 1622 as an ambassador sent by her brother, King Ngola Mbandi, to negotiate with the Portuguese governor in Luanda.

A famous story tells that when she entered the room, the governor sat on a chair but offered her only a mat on the floor. Nzinga signalled to a servant, who knelt on hands and knees, and she sat on the servant's back, speaking to the governor as an equal.

After her brother's death she took power, though some men argued a woman could not rule. When the Portuguese backed rivals, she moved east and conquered the kingdom of Matamba, building a new power base. She formed alliances with the Imbangala warriors and even with the Dutch, who were fighting Portugal.

She was a skilled diplomat and military commander, leading troops into battle into her sixties. In 1657 she finally signed a peace treaty with Portugal. She died in 1663, aged about 80.

Nzinga's legacy is complex, as her kingdoms were also involved in the slave trade, as most powers of the region were. But in Angola today she is honoured as a national heroine and symbol of resistance.

en.title: The Tokugawa shogunate begins
en.text:
On 24 March 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu received the title of shogun from the emperor of Japan. He set up his government in the small castle town of Edo, today's Tokyo, beginning more than 250 years of peace known as the Edo period.

For over a century before, Japan had been torn by civil war between rival warlords, the daimyo. Three great leaders gradually reunited the country: Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and finally Tokugawa Ieyasu, who defeated his rivals at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

The emperor in Kyoto remained a sacred figure, but real power belonged to the shogun. The Tokugawa controlled the daimyo through a clever system: each lord had to spend every other year in Edo and leave his family there as hostages. The costly journeys kept the daimyo busy and loyal.

Society was organised into ranks: samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Christianity was banned after a rebellion in 1637, and from the 1630s the shogunate restricted foreign contact. Only Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed, at Nagasaki.

Yet Japan flourished. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people. Literacy spread. Kabuki theatre, haiku poetry, and woodblock prints such as Hokusai's "Great Wave" were born in this era.

In 1853 American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry arrived and forced Japan to open to trade. The shogunate collapsed in 1868, power returned to the emperor in the Meiji Restoration, and Japan rapidly modernised.

en.title: The American Declaration of Independence
en.text:
On 4 July 1776, delegates of thirteen British colonies in North America, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence. They announced that the colonies were now free and independent states: the United States of America.

Tensions with Britain had grown for more than a decade over taxes imposed by the British Parliament, in which the colonists had no representatives. The slogan "no taxation without representation" spread. Fighting began in April 1775 at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts.

The Declaration was drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. Its most famous lines state that all men are created equal and have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments get their power from the consent of the governed.

Those words were powerful but did not apply to everyone. Jefferson himself enslaved more than 600 people during his life, and around one in five people in the colonies were enslaved Africans and their descendants. Women could not vote, and Native American nations were treated as enemies. Black Americans such as Frederick Douglass later used the Declaration's own words to demand freedom.

With help from France, Spain and the Netherlands, the Americans won the war, which ended in 1783. The Constitution, written in 1787, created a federal republic with an elected president.
